messages.content: My best friend Danny is getting married Saturday and I'm the best man. We met in seventh grade when he gave me half his sandwich after I dropped mine in the cafeteria. I want a toast that's funny but actually means something. Help me write it.

Here is a toast built on that sandwich, because it is the whole friendship in one gesture:

"For those who don't know, Danny and I met in seventh grade, twenty seconds after my lunch tray hit the cafeteria floor. He looked at the wreckage, looked at his sandwich, and tore it in half. No speech. No hesitation. Half.

That is who Danny is. He has been tearing things in half for me ever since: the driving on road trips, the rent the year I lost my job, the last slice of anything, every single time. He never keeps score because, in his head, there was never anything to score.

Priya, you are getting the half-sandwich guy. The man who will give you the better portion without noticing he did it. And Danny, after twenty years of receiving, it is my genuine honor to finally say this in public: my half is yours too. It always was.

To Danny and Priya."

Delivery notes: it runs about ninety seconds spoken, which is the sweet spot. Land the pause before "my half is yours too" — that is the line people will remember. Do not add more jokes after it; end on the warmth.

My grandfather died last week at 91. He was a quiet man who fixed things for the whole street — radios, fences, a kid's bike chain, anything. He never talked about himself. I have to speak at the funeral and I don't want the usual clichés. Can you help me find words that sound like him?

A quiet man deserves a eulogy in his own register — plain, specific, and built out of the work of his hands. Here is a draft shaped around what he actually did:

"Grandad never made a speech in his life, so he would want this kept short and useful.

If you lived on our street, something in your house once passed through his hands. A radio that came back to life. A fence that stood straight again. A bike chain, fixed on the pavement while a kid waited, and fixed properly, not well-enough. He kept a tin of screws sorted by size for sixty years, because you never knew what somebody would need.

He taught me that love is mostly a practical thing. It shows up. It brings its tools. It does not make a fuss about being there.

The street is quieter this week. But every gate that still swings true on our road is swinging because of him, and I think that is exactly the memorial he would have chosen."

Two craft notes: the sorted tin of screws does more work than any adjective could — keep it. And read the last line slowly; a room full of neighbours will be picturing their own gates. If you tear up, let it happen on "brings its tools" — pausing there looks like emphasis, not breakdown.

We're having a little welcome lunch for a new hire, Priya Nair, who starts Monday on our support team. My manager asked me to say a few words when she arrives. Keep it short and warm — I don't know her well yet.

Short and warm is exactly right for day one. Try this, standing up with a smile and nothing in your hands:

"Before we eat, thirty seconds. This is Priya Nair, who starts with us today on the support team. Priya, two things you should know. First, this team answers its own questions for about a week and then we all start asking you — that's the natural order, don't fight it. Second, everything you're unsure about this month, we were unsure about once too, and most of us wrote it down nowhere, so ask loudly and often.

We're glad you're here. Lunch is on the company, the good biscuits go fast, and your desk is the one with the plant we haven't killed yet. Welcome to the team."

It works because it does three jobs in forty-five seconds: it names her properly, it gives her permission to ask questions, and it makes the room laugh once, at the team's expense rather than hers. Say her name twice — new people listen for whether the room has learned it.

My mum turns 80 next month. She's sharp, funny, and allergic to sentimentality — she'll heckle anything mushy. I want to say something at her party that honours her without getting booed by the guest of honour herself.

Then the tribute has to be smuggled inside the comedy — she gets honoured, but on her terms. Something like this:

"Mum has given me strict instructions: no crying, no poems, and absolutely no journey metaphors. So I'll keep this factual.

Fact one: she can still beat everyone in this room at Scrabble, and she does not let children win, because, and I quote, 'they'll learn nothing from charity.' Fact two: she has read more books than the rest of us combined and remembers all of them, including the ones she'd like to forget. Fact three: when Dad died, she held this whole family together with soup, sarcasm, and a diary organised like a military campaign.

Eighty years, and the sharpest person I know is still the one who taught me to argue properly — mostly by winning.

Happy birthday, Mum. Heckle away; I've finished."

The structure matters: the opening joke buys you the room, the three facts carry the love in disguise, and fact three is placed late enough that she'll feel it before she can deflect it. Invite the heckle at the end — it lets her respond in character, which is the gift she'd actually choose.

I'm retiring after 34 years as a high-school physics teacher. The school is giving me a send-off and I have to speak. I don't want a list of thank-yous or a greatest-hits reel. I want to say something true about the work. Can you help me shape it?

Here is a shape that honours the work instead of the résumé — about three minutes spoken:

"People keep asking what I'll miss, and they expect me to say the students, and I will — but not in the way they mean.

I'll miss the exact moment a face changes. You've seen it if you've taught anything: a kid is looking at a problem like it's written in a dead language, and then something connects, and the whole face reorganises. I have seen that moment perhaps ten thousand times in thirty-four years, and I am here to tell you it does not get old. It is the best seat in the world and I have had it for free.

I taught physics, but the subject was always a pretext. The real curriculum was: the world makes sense if you look at it carefully, and you are capable of looking carefully. Some of my students became engineers. Some became plumbers, nurses, parents, one memorable concert pianist. All of them, I hope, kept the habit of asking what the evidence says.

To my colleagues: the staffroom carried me more years than I carried it. To the students still out there wondering if room 12 mattered — it did. You were the experiment that always worked.

Thank you. Now, somebody else gets the good seat."

The closing line hands the room to your successor instead of ending on yourself — that is what will make colleagues quote it afterwards. If there is a specific colleague who carried you in a hard year, name them in the staffroom sentence; one real name outweighs a paragraph of general gratitude.

Our daughter graduates from university next week — first in our family to do it. Everything I draft sounds like a greeting card. I want to say something at the family dinner that is actually about her, not about graduates in general.

The greeting-card trap is writing about Graduates. Write about her instead — the specific evidence of who she already is. A shape like this:

"Everyone will tell you this week that the world is full of possibility, which is true and also useless. So instead, some things I know, because I've watched them.

I know you finished a dissertation in a house where the heating broke in February, wrapped in two blankets, and didn't mention it until it was handed in. I know you rang your brother from the library steps the night before his exams, every night, because he was nervous and you decided his nerves mattered more than your sleep. I know you worked Saturdays in a café for three years and the regulars asked for you by name.

A degree certifies what you studied. It says nothing about the blankets, the phone calls, or the café. We were there for those. That's the person we're proud of — the degree is just the part that fits in a frame.

Whatever comes next, you already know how to do hard things in cold rooms for people you love. That's most of life, love. The rest is details."

Notice the recipe: three witnessed facts, each small, each verifiable by the family in the room — then one sentence about what they prove. Swap in your own three facts and the speech becomes un-stealable; nobody else on earth could give it.

Six months ago my neighbours, the Okafor family, took me in for two weeks when my flat flooded — fed me, gave me their spare room, the works. They're having a housewarming at their new place and asked me to say a few words. I want to thank them properly, in public, without making it awkward.

Public thanks works when it is specific, brief, and turns the compliment outward to the room. Try this:

"I should explain why I, of all people, got asked to speak at this housewarming: because I have already lived with the Okafors, and I can give you the review.

When my flat flooded in March, they took me in for two weeks. Not the sofa — the spare room. Not leftovers — a place set at the table, every night, with my name effectively on it. Mrs Okafor learnt how I take my tea by day two. Mr Okafor drove me to view replacement flats on his day off and talked me out of the one with the damp wall, which turned out to be excellent advice.

So I can tell this neighbourhood, with evidence: you have not just gained a family on this street. You have gained the people who will notice when your curtains stay closed one morning too long.

To the Okafors — thank you, and may this house be as good to you as you were to me under emergency conditions."

The line "may this house be as good to you" repays the debt in the toast itself, which is what makes it graceful rather than awkward. Keep it under two minutes; gratitude spoken too long starts to sound like it's about the speaker.

My parents are celebrating 50 years of marriage. People keep calling it a fairy tale but honestly they bicker constantly, always have. I want anniversary words that are honest about that and still moving.

Honesty is the better tribute — fifty years of bickering is fifty years of staying in the conversation. A shape:

"Fifty years. People will use the word 'fairytale' today, so let me correct the record: my parents have disagreed, out loud, about the correct way to load a dishwasher, drive to the coast, and pronounce 'scone', for half a century.

But here is what I noticed growing up, and what I understand now. They never once let an argument be the last word of the day. Dad would be mid-grumble and still put the kettle on for two. Mum could be furious and still leave his reading glasses where he'd find them. The bickering was weather. The small kindnesses were climate.

They taught me that love is not the absence of friction. It's a long practice of staying at the table — arguing about the scones, pouring the tea anyway.

Fifty years at the table. Mum, Dad — the kettle's on us tonight."

The weather/climate contrast is the engine; it lets the room laugh in recognition first and then feel the weight of it. If there's a famous family argument — a legendary one everyone knows — name it in the list of three. Shared recognition is what turns a toast into a family heirloom.

My grandparents married in June 1976 and I want to open their anniversary toast with the exact number of days they've been married as of this Saturday, which is 27 June 2026. Can you work it out and help me use it in a line?

Here is the arithmetic first: fifty full years from 27 June 1976 to 27 June 2026 is 18,262 days — that count includes the twelve leap days that fell inside the marriage, which is a detail worth savouring.

And here is the line to open with:

"Eighteen thousand, two hundred and sixty-two days. That's how long these two have been married — including twelve leap days, which feels right, because this marriage has always made room for the extra day. In that time they have had roughly eighteen thousand breakfasts together, and Grandad still makes Grandma's toast the wrong way, and she still eats it, and that, ladies and gentlemen, is the entire secret, and it cannot be improved upon."

Why the number works as an opener: it sounds enormous and faintly absurd, which gets the laugh, and then the breakfasts translate it back into ordinary life, which is where the feeling lives. If you want a second figure for later in the toast, the same span is 438,288 hours — but use only one big number. Two statistics and it stops being a toast and becomes a report.
We just moved into our first house and my sister is coming over for dinner Friday — the first guest. I want to say a tiny toast before we eat, nothing fancy. What could I say?

Tiny is perfect for a first dinner — the house is the occasion, so let the toast be small enough to match. Try this, glasses up, before anyone sits down properly:

"Okay, quick one, because the food's getting cold and so is this house until the heating beds in. To first dinners in first houses: to this table, which we assembled ourselves and which only wobbles a bit; to you, our first guest, who gets the good chair and the honest tour, including the cupboard we're not opening yet; and to every meal that comes after this one, in this room, for as long as we're lucky enough to have it. Eat."

Thirty seconds, three beats: the house, the guest, the future. The wobbling table and the forbidden cupboard do the real work — a first-home toast should admit the place is imperfect, because that's the charm the guest came to see. Don't apologise for the house anywhere else in the evening; the toast already did it, charmingly, once.

My close friend Sara just had her first baby, a boy named Tomás. I'm visiting tomorrow and I'd like to say something when I first meet him — not a speech, just words that mark it. Everything I think of sounds like a card.

Meeting a baby needs about four sentences, spoken to the parents as much as to him. Something like this, when you're holding him or standing at the cot:

"Well. Hello, Tomás. You've been expected.

Sara, I have known you through exams, heartbreaks, one truly terrible flat, and a wedding — and I have never seen you look the way you looked when you said his name just now. So before anything else: he's landed well. He has you.

Tomás, your only job for about a year is eating and sleeping, and the reviews so far are excellent. Your mum's job is the same, and we'll make sure she does it — that's what the rest of us are for.

Welcome to the world, small man. You are already so loved it's slightly inefficient."

Two things make it land: it honours the mother before it charms at the baby, which is the correct order in week one; and it quietly assigns the friends a job — feeding and protecting the mother's rest — which turns sentiment into a promise she'll actually remember at 3 a.m. in February.

My younger brother is moving to New Zealand next month for work — probably for years. We're having a farewell dinner and as the older sibling I keep being handed the microphone. I want to say goodbye in a way that doesn't turn the whole evening into a funeral.

The trick is to aim the speech at his future, not at your loss — grief gets one line, not the whole toast. A shape:

"House rules for this speech: nobody cries until dessert, and Daniel is paying for dessert, so plan accordingly.

When Daniel was nine he announced he was running away and got as far as the end of the street with a backpack containing one jumper and forty biscuits. He came home because it rained. I mention this because it's the same traveller: overprepared on snacks, underprepared for weather, completely certain about the destination.

New Zealand doesn't know what's arriving. It is getting the brother who rings to check you got home safe, who learnt to fix a bike chain from YouTube to help a neighbour's kid, who will absolutely be the person on his new street who knows where the fuse box is by week two.

We'll miss him here. That's the one line of that, and it's true, and it's done.

Daniel: go well. Eat before the weather. And ring us — we'll be checking you got there safe."

The callback at the end — reversing the family ritual so the stay-behinds now check on him — gives the room a tender final beat that is still forward-facing. The "one line of that, and it's done" move is worth stealing for any farewell: naming your rationing of sadness gives you permission to feel it fully for exactly one sentence.

I'm opening our village fete this year — I run the hall committee. It's a small thing, 200 people on a field, but I want the opening words to actually gather people rather than just announce the tombola. Any help?

An opening gathers people when it names what the gathering is for before it names what's on. Two minutes, roughly this:

"Welcome, everyone — look at this field. A year ago this was just the wettest patch of grass in the parish, and today it's got bunting on it, so we're already winning.

A fete like this doesn't happen by accident. It happens because Mrs Whitfield has made four hundred scones and won't discuss it, because the cricket club lent us their benches and their strongest teenagers, because the Patel family have run the plant stall for eleven years and the tomatoes have a waiting list, and because a lot of people did small jobs nobody will ever thank them for by name. Consider this the thanking.

Everything raised today goes to the hall roof, which currently lets in weather in two places — you'll find the buckets, they're part of the tour.

So: eat, spend, enter the raffle, lose gracefully at the coconut shy. This village looks after its own, and today it does it with cake. The fete is open."

Notice the order: welcome, gratitude with real names and numbers, the cause made concrete (two buckets, not "much-needed repairs"), then permission to have fun. If you open with logistics, you get an audience; open with people and you get a community that happens to also buy raffle tickets.

The wedding was last weekend and it was perfect. I want to write thank-you notes to the people who helped — not generic ones. My aunt Rosa did all the flowers from her own garden. Can you help me write hers, and tell me how to make the others feel just as specific?

Aunt Rosa's first, then the method:

"Dear Aunt Rosa,

Everybody photographed the flowers. What they couldn't photograph was you, in your garden at six in the morning for a week, cutting the good roses — the ones you've defended from greenfly like a general — so that our wedding would smell of your garden and not a warehouse.

When I walked in and saw the table arrangements I cried before I'd even found Tom. You grew our wedding, Aunt Rosa. It took you a whole season and you made it look like an afternoon.

We have dried one of the buttonholes and it's going in a frame, with your name on the back, where the credit belongs.

All our love, always."

Now the method, because it scales to every other note: name the invisible labour, not the visible gift. Anyone can write "thanks for the flowers." Only you can write about the 6 a.m. cutting and the greenfly war. For each helper, ask: what did this cost them that nobody saw? Time, sleep, a season, a day off, their nerves. Thank them for that. One true sentence of invisible labour per note, and no two notes will read alike — because no two people gave the same hidden thing.

A colleague, Ingrid, is leaving our research lab after 19 years to run a bakery — a complete change. I'm giving the farewell speech. She's formidable and dry-witted and would hate anything soppy, but I also genuinely want to honour what she built here. Help me thread it.

Dry on the surface, load-bearing underneath — write it the way she is. A shape:

"Nineteen years ago, Ingrid arrived in this lab and found our data archive in a state she described, in her first week, as 'archaeological.' She then spent two decades quietly becoming the reason any of us can find anything, reproduce anything, or defend anything we've published. There are papers from this group that exist because Ingrid asked one question in a meeting: 'And where is that written down?' 

She has now decided to apply the same terrifying standards to bread.

People keep calling this a loss for the lab, and it is, but I refuse to make it sound like an ending, because Ingrid doesn't do endings — she does handovers. The archive is documented. The systems have manuals. Somewhere in those manuals, I guarantee, is a note that says 'do not improvise this part,' and we will obey it forever, out of respect and fear.

Ingrid: this lab runs on your rigour. The bakery is about to. Go and be formidable somewhere warmer. And when the first loaf fails, we all know what you'll say: where is that written down?"

The repeated line is the tribute — it turns her professional fingerprint into the room's shared memory of her. Keep the ending brisk; a dry-witted person's farewell should exit like she would: on time, without lingering at the door.
My daughter just passed her driving test, first try. We're doing a little family tea tonight. I want to say a few proud words without embarrassing her to death — she's 17.

At seventeen, the toast should be short, proud, and mostly aimed at the adults so she can just grin at the cake. Try this:

"Quick toast before tea, and I promise, Sophie, it's short. Today this one passed her driving test, first attempt, in the rain, with the examiner who apparently never smiles. He smiled. Slightly.

Sophie, you practised in the dark after school, you mastered the hill start that defeats grown men, and you did not once cry at a roundabout, which is more than I managed at your age.

We're proud of you. The car keys, however, remain a subject of ongoing negotiation, and your brother has already been told he is not insured on anything, ever, including the future.

To Sophie — safest driver in the family, as of today, officially."

It works because the pride is carried by evidence (rain, the hill start, the unsmiling examiner) rather than adjectives, and the joke at the end is aimed at the keys and the brother, not at her. Keep your glass raised briefly and sit down fast — brevity is the whole gift at that age.

My dad is being given a community award for running the youth football club for 25 years. They've asked me to introduce him. He'll be mortified. Two minutes, tops — help me make it count and not kill him with embarrassment.

Two minutes, and protect him by aiming the praise at the work and the kids, with him almost as a bystander. Like this:

"For twenty-five years, every Saturday morning of the season, in weather that closed schools, my dad has unlocked a changing room, put the nets up, and refereed arguments about offside with the seriousness of a man defusing something.

In that time, roughly nine hundred local kids have played for this club. Some are in this room. Some now bring their own kids on Saturdays, which he pretends not to find moving.

He kept the subs at two pounds for a decade because, and this is a direct quote, 'no kid sits out because of money.' He drove home whichever child was left waiting, every time, without commentary.

He will hate this award because he thinks the club is the point. He's right, and it's also the reason he's getting it.

Dad — the nets are up. This one's yours."

"The nets are up" gives him a familiar image to stand inside while a room applauds, which is the kindest thing an introduction can do for a mortified man. Speak to the room, not at him, and only look at him on the final line — that rationing of eye contact is what keeps men like him composed.
Quick one — my wife and I got married on 14 February 2015 and I want the card for our anniversary this year, 14 February 2026, to say how many years it is. I'm terrible at counting. Help?

Eleven years — your card should say 11th anniversary. And since a number alone is a bit bare in a card, here is a line to go with it:

"Eleven years since a registrar's office, your cold hands, and that terrible coffee afterwards. I'd change the coffee. Nothing else."

If you want the traditional gift angle, the 11th anniversary is steel — which sounds unromantic until you write it properly: "Eleven years: steel. Strong, bright, and it doesn't rust. Rather like us on our better days." Pick whichever sounds more like the two of you; the registrar-and-coffee line is warmer, the steel line is wittier. Either way, write it by hand — a correct number in your own handwriting beats a printed card at any year count.

My twin sister and I turn 40 together next week — obviously. I'm speaking at our joint party. I want to say something about being a twin that isn't the usual 'built-in best friend' stuff. We actually weren't close as teenagers and only got close in our thirties.

The honest arc is the interesting one — use it. A shape:

"People assume twins arrive pre-assembled as best friends. Ruth and I would like to correct the record: for roughly fifteen years we were more like two countries sharing a border and a bathroom. We had different friends, different music, and a treaty about the phone that was violated weekly.

Then life started happening — jobs, breakups, our dad's illness, all the weather of your thirties — and I discovered something. The person who has known every version of you, including the ones you'd rather forget, turns out to be the one person you never have to explain yourself to. Somewhere in that decade, the border came down.

So this isn't a toast to being twins. It's a toast to becoming friends on purpose, late, which I now think is the better story. Anyone can be born close. We chose it.

Ruth: happy fortieth. The treaty is officially retired. You may use my phone."

The phone callback closes the treaty joke from the opening — callbacks are what make a speech feel crafted rather than assembled. Keep the teenage years funny rather than bitter; the room should hear distance that was survived, not grievance that survived.
Our book club has been running for ten years — six of us, monthly, we've read about 100 books. We're having an anniversary dinner and I want to mark it with a few words. Nothing grand, just right.

Ten years of a book club is really ten years of six people keeping an appointment with each other — the books are the excuse. Words like these:

"Ten years, six members, and by our own rough count about a hundred books — of which we finished, collectively, perhaps eighty, and lied about the rest with great confidence.

But here's what I actually want to say. In ten years, this group has carried its members through two divorces, one redundancy, four house moves, a baby, a bereavement, and the novel with the unreliable narrator that nearly ended us. Every month, whatever was happening, there was a Tuesday where someone had made tea and read the chapters and was expecting you.

We came for the books. We stayed because a standing appointment with people who know your whole story is one of the great underrated structures of a life.

To the next hundred books — and to finishing at least ninety of them."

The confession about the unfinished books is essential: it gives the room its laugh early, and it makes the sincere middle section believable, because a speaker who admits the small fraud is trusted with the large truth.

I need to give the eulogy for my mother. She was a nurse for 40 years, on night shifts mostly. She was brisk, unsentimental, and the person everyone in a crisis actually wanted in the room. I keep writing things that sound soft and she wasn't soft. Help me write it hard and loving, like her.

Then the eulogy should have her posture: upright, practical, no wasted motion. A draft:

"Mum did nights for forty years. While the rest of the world slept, she was awake in the lit corridors, and I have come to think that tells you everything about her: she took the shift nobody wanted, at the hours when people are most frightened, and she was brisk in those corridors because frightened people do not need your tears. They need your competence. She gave them that, ten thousand nights of it.

At home she was the same. She did not do fuss. When I failed my exams she made tea, asked for the facts, and drew up a plan on the back of an envelope. When Dad was dying she nursed him with the same hands she'd used on strangers for decades, and the only difference was that she held his a moment longer at the end of each task.

People have said to me this week that she was an angel. She would have hated that. She was not an angel. She was a nurse, which is better: angels are born, nurses are made, out of discipline and staying awake and showing up.

She showed up. For strangers, for us, for the worst hours of people's lives. The corridors are darker without her. But somewhere there are thousands of people who got through their worst night because she was on it, and that is not a soft legacy. It is a hard one, and a huge one, and it is hers."

The angel correction is the heart of it — mourners will nod, because everyone who knew her will recognise the refusal. If you include one envelope, one tea, one specific night of your own, it becomes hers alone. Keep your voice flat and let the sentences do the work; brisk delivery is itself a tribute to a brisk woman.

My little brother just got his first job — shelf-stacking at a supermarket while he's at college. Family dinner Sunday and I want to toast him without it sounding like a big deal speech. Just a proud big-sister moment.

Small occasion, small toast — the pride lands better when the speech doesn't inflate it. Try this, raised glass, thirty seconds:

"To Marcus: first job, first payslip incoming, and — I have checked — already an expert on which aisle everything is in, including the things nobody should buy.

You applied, you interviewed in a shirt that I ironed, and you got it yourself. That's the whole announcement. Everything else in your working life is just this, repeated at higher stakes: show up, be useful, be the one who knows where things are.

Proud of you. Your round next Sunday — you're a working man now, and the family has unanimously voted that wages change everything."

The closing joke does two jobs: it welcomes him into the adults' economy, and it keeps the moment light enough that a little brother can actually enjoy being toasted instead of enduring it. Aim all the sincerity into the middle sentence — "you got it yourself" — because that's the part he'll remember when the job gets boring in month two.

We're christening our daughter on Sunday — her name is Wren. The vicar lets family say a few words. I want something brief that explains why we chose the name without sounding like a nature documentary.

Brief, warm, and one good reason is enough. Something like this:

"A few people have asked about the name, so, briefly: a wren is a very small bird with an enormous song. It weighs almost nothing and it can fill a garden. The old stories call it the king of birds — not because it's the biggest, but because it was the cleverest, and rode up to the sky on the eagle's back.

We liked that for her. Small is not the same as quiet. Clever counts. And you don't have to be the largest creature in the sky to end up highest.

Wren, you are four months old and already extremely good at being heard, so the name is holding up well.

Welcome, little one. The garden is yours."

It works because the explanation doubles as a blessing without announcing itself as one — the three short lessons (small isn't quiet, clever counts, you can ride high) are hopes for her disguised as facts about a bird. Keep it to that length; at a christening the baby sets the schedule, and finishing before she objects is its own kind of elegance.

My husband is being promoted to partner at his law firm. There's a dinner with the other partners and I've been asked — as the spouse — to say a few words, which apparently is tradition. I know nothing about law dinners. I want to be proud, funny, and not embarrass him in front of people who bill by the hour.

Then be the only person in the room not talking like a lawyer — that contrast is your charm. A shape:

"I should declare my interest: I am the person who has lived with this man's billable hours for eleven years, including the ones that happened at our kitchen table, on two holidays, and during the birth of our first child, from which he was technically present.

What the firm is getting as a partner, I can testify, is this: a man who reads the small print on his own family's insurance for pleasure. Who prepares for a school parents' evening like a deposition. Who cannot lose an argument at home because he takes notes.

But also — and the firm may not know this yet — a man who answered his phone at midnight for a junior colleague in tears, talked her down for an hour, and never mentioned it again. That's the partner I'd want, if I were ever unwise enough to need one.

James: the kitchen table is proud of you. Try to be home for its next sitting."

The structure protects you both: the jokes are about his habits, which he owns happily, and the midnight phone call is the single serious fact, placed third so it arrives after the room is warmed. Spouses' speeches fail by gushing or by roasting; this does neither — it testifies, which is, appropriately, the one legal skill a spouse genuinely has.

Our community choir is celebrating its 25th anniversary with a concert, and as the chair I need to say a few words before the final song. Most of the founding members are in their 70s and 80s now. Something that honours them and the music.

Place the founders in the room, not in the past — they're sitting there. A shape:

"Before the last song, look around this choir for a moment. Twenty-five years ago, eleven people stood in a cold school hall and sang to an audience of nine, four of whom were related to them.

Some of those eleven are on this stage tonight. Margaret has sung alto for all twenty-five years and has missed, by her own count, three rehearsals, two of which she disputes. The rest of us are their echo — every singer who joined since walked into a sound that already existed, built by people who kept showing up on wet Tuesday nights when it would have been easier not to.

A choir is a promise a town makes to itself: that once a week, whatever else is happening, some of its people will stand together and make one sound out of many voices. Twenty-five years of Tuesdays. That's the anniversary.

Founders — this last song is the one you sang at the first concert. Take us home."

Ending by handing the final song to the founders converts the tribute into an act instead of a description — the room hears the 25 years rather than just hearing about them. If you know the exact first-concert song, name it; specificity about repertoire is the detail singers themselves will treasure.

My best mate has just come out of a long illness — he's well again, back at work part-time. A few of us are having a small dinner to mark it. I want to say something that celebrates without making the illness the whole evening or pretending it didn't happen.

The balance is: one honest sentence about the illness, then a speech about him. Like this:

"I want to say one thing properly and then get on with dinner. This year was frightening, and there were weeks when this table didn't know what it was allowed to hope for. Rob got through it the way he does everything: stubbornly, with terrible jokes at the worst moments, and by making the nurses laugh when laughing was not the obvious option.

That's the sentence. It's said, it's true, and now it's done — because Rob did not spend a year being ill in order to spend the rest of his life being introduced as the man who was.

So here's the actual toast: to Rob, back at work, back at this table, back to being beaten at pool by me — a tradition this group held in trust for him and now returns, in full working order.

Mate: it's good to have you back in the ordinary. The ordinary missed you."

"Back in the ordinary" is the phrase that does the healing work — after a year of hospitals, ordinary life is the luxury, and naming it as the prize lets the table celebrate the mundane on purpose. Keep the illness to that single middle passage; if anyone else wants to say more, they can, but the host setting the ration gives everyone else permission to relax.

My gran's care home is doing a little party for her 95th birthday. They've asked family to say a few words. She gets tired quickly so it needs to be short, and she loves a laugh more than a tear. Ideas?

Short, funny, and built for a woman who'd rather laugh — ninety seconds at most:

"Ninety-five years. Gran has outlived three kings, fourteen prime ministers, and every single one of her houseplants, which she maintains were 'already dying when I got them.'

She has strong opinions, a boyfriend in the dining room she pretends not to have, and she still wins the quiz by knowing things nobody taught her.

Gran, the family position is this: we are not saying you're old. We are saying you are the most experienced person we know, and we would like the recipe — for the longevity, not the trifle. We have tried the trifle. The trifle is not the secret.

Happy birthday, Gran. Save us some cake."

For a 95th, jokes about endurance land better than jokes about age, and the houseplant line gives her a comeback, which is what a sharp nonagenarian actually wants from a speech — something to bat back. Say it to her, not about her, and finish while she's still fresh: at that age, a short speech is a form of respect.

I'm best man for my brother Tom next month. His fiancée Aisha's family is quite traditional and there will be about 150 guests, many of whom I don't know. I want the speech to welcome her family properly, not just roast my brother for seven minutes.

Welcoming the other family is the mark of a best-man speech that grew up. A structure that works in a mixed room:

"For those I haven't met: I'm Tom's brother, which means I have known him at his worst — I have the photographs, and they are not in this speech, because I also have to live near him.

I want to say something to Aisha's family first, because it matters more than the jokes. You are not losing anything today and neither are we — but I know a wedding can feel, to the people who raised the bride, like a handing over. So from our side of the room: we see what you built. Aisha's kindness, her steadiness, the way she has looked after my brother since long before today — that didn't happen by accident. It came from your house. Thank you for it, and welcome to ours. It's yours now too.

Tom: you were a decent man before Aisha. You are a better one in her weather. Keep the photographs out of it and I'll keep this short — to Tom and Aisha."

Two craft points: put the welcome before the best jokes about your brother, because the room reads order as priority; and keep the roast to the single photographs threat rather than actual stories — in a room of 150 near-strangers, a threat is funnier than evidence and far safer. If Aisha's family has a particular custom of welcome, echo it in one line — ask Tom beforehand, and get it exactly right.

A woman I mentored for six years, Leila, has just won a major professional award in our field — architecture. There's a small dinner. I want to toast her without making it sound like I'm taking credit for her, which mentors at microphones tend to do.

The discipline is: your pride gets one sentence, her work gets the rest. Like this:

"Six years ago Leila joined our studio and asked, in her first month, why we always did a certain thing a certain way. It was a very good question. It was such a good question that it took the studio about two years to fully admit it.

I have been introduced tonight as her mentor, so let me correct the record in the traditional way: by describing what I actually did. I answered questions. I opened two doors. I once reviewed a set of drawings at midnight and found one error, which she has never let me forget. That is the complete inventory.

Everything else — the competition entries nobody expected her to win, the building that now stands on the old market site, this award — is hers, built out of the habit she arrived with: asking why, and not accepting the first answer.

Leila: the studio still does that thing differently because of your question. The profession is about to. Congratulations — entirely, demonstrably, yours."

"That is the complete inventory" is the line that clears you: enumerating how small your contribution was is funnier and more credible than disclaiming credit in general terms. Then the toast returns to her founding habit, which is the true through-line of her career — mentors are remembered best by mentees when they hand the whole story back.

My neighbours just finished building an extension after two years of planning rows, builders, and mud. They're having a small gathering in the new room and jokingly asked me to 'officially open' it. I want to play along properly — a little ribbon moment with words.

Lean into the ceremony — mock-official only works if you commit. Something like this, scissors in hand:

"Ladies and gentlemen, neighbours, and long-suffering residents of this street: it falls to me, as the person who watched most of this project from behind a curtain with a cup of tea, to say a few words.

For two years we have lived alongside the Great Extension: through the skip era, the scaffolding era, the famous Portaloo Period, and the winter of the tarpaulin. We have heard every saw. We forgive all of them, because look at this room.

By the powers vested in me by absolutely nobody, I declare this extension open. May the roof never leak, may the Wi-Fi reach the far corner, and may Helen and Marcus enjoy the radical luxury of a room that was worth the Portaloo.

Cut the ribbon. Mind the new paint. Tea is, I believe, through there — through the new bit."

The joke structure borrows the real grammar of openings — eras, declarations, blessings — and the blessings at the end are secretly sincere, which is why the room will cheer. Name the worst phase of the build by its household nickname if it has one; nothing delights builders'-hell survivors like hearing the Portaloo Period entered into the official record.

I have to speak at the funeral of my oldest friend, Margaret, who died at 84. We were friends for 61 years — met at school. I don't want a biography; everyone knows the facts. I want to say what 61 years of friendship actually is. I can hold it together for about three minutes.

Three minutes, and write about the friendship itself, not the life — the room knows the life. A draft:

"Margaret and I met in 1965, in a classroom neither of us remembers properly, and we have been in each other's lives every week since. Sixty-one years. People ask what the secret of a friendship like that is, as if we knew. We didn't. We just never stopped. Through marriages, divorces, children, illnesses, one long estrangement in the eighties over something neither of us could later name — we never stopped.

Here is what sixty-one years actually is. It is a person who knows what you mean before you finish the sentence. It is a voice on the phone that requires no introduction, no catching up, no performance. It is the last witness. Margaret was the last person alive who remembered me at eleven, at twenty, at forty — all the selves I have been are stored, now, in one fewer place.

I am not going to tell you she is at peace, because she would have had views about me saying that too.

I will tell you this: I was lucky in the central way a person can be lucky. I had a witness. Thank you for witnessing her with me today."

"The last witness" is the truth at the centre of old friendship, and naming it gives the whole room — most of whom will have known her for less time — a way to understand what you specifically have lost. If your voice goes, it will go at "one fewer place"; pause there, breathe, and continue flatly. Flat is fine. Sixty-one years does not need volume.

My son's football team just won their under-11s league and I'm the assistant coach. The head coach wants me to say a few words at the little awards night. The kids are 10 and 11, attention span of goldfish. Keep me brief and fun.

For under-11s, ninety seconds is a long speech and jokes beat wisdom two to one. Try this:

"Right, listen up, champions — short speech, then pizza, in that order, and the pizza is watching.

At the start of the season we could not pass in a straight line. Our first match, the ball spent more time in the car park than on the pitch. And look at you now: league winners. You ran, you passed, you encouraged each other — mostly — and nobody, in the entire season, cried at a referee. Except Coach Dan. Once. We don't talk about it.

Every one of you gets a medal tonight, and every one of you earned it, including our goalkeeper, who faced four shots all season and saved them all like a wall with gloves.

You were the best team to stand in the rain with. Champions — pizza."

Name the improvement, not just the trophy — kids remember being told they got better at something specific long after the medal is in a drawer. And put the pizza in the first line: announcing the reward up front is the only reliable way to hold a room of ten-year-olds, and the adults will quietly thank you too.

My wife and I are renewing our vows after 25 years — small ceremony, just family and a few friends. I want to say my own words rather than repeat the standard ones. The honest truth is the second decade was hard and the recent years have been the best. Can that be said at a vow renewal?

Yes — and said well, it's the only version worth hearing, because everyone in the room over thirty knows it's true. A shape:

"Twenty-five years ago I stood in a register office and promised things I didn't understand, to a woman I loved in the way you love at twenty-six: completely and with no information.

Today I know more. I know that years six to fifteen nearly did for us — the small children, the money, the tiredness, the two of us becoming people the other one hadn't met yet. I know we stayed in some seasons out of habit and in others out of stubbornness, and I know that somewhere in the staying, it turned. The last five years have been the best of my life, and they are not the years I would have predicted at the altar.

So these vows are different. Last time I promised forever, which is easy to say and impossible to picture. This time I promise the specific things: the morning tea. The honest answer. The hand on the back in a hard room. Staying in the conversation when the conversation is the last place I want to be.

Clare — I choose you again, with information this time. It is a much better choosing."

"With information this time" is the line the whole speech hangs on — it converts the hard decade from an embarrassment into evidence. Keep the specific promises genuinely small (tea, honesty, a hand on the back): at a renewal, tiny vows are more moving than grand ones because the room can see they're load-bearing.

My parents married on 3 May 1986. For their 40th anniversary party on 3 May 2026 I want a banner line with the number of months they've been married, and to double-check the years too. Can you compute both and give me a way to use them?

Both figures check out: 3 May 1986 to 3 May 2026 is exactly 40 years, and 40 years at 12 months a year is 480 months.

For the banner, the months figure is actually the better choice — it sounds bigger and it surprises people. Something like:

"480 MONTHS. 2 KIDS. 1 HOUSE. STILL ARGUING ABOUT THE THERMOSTAT."

And if you're saying a few words as well as hanging a banner, the months open a toast beautifully:

"Four hundred and eighty months. That's how the tenancy of this marriage reads, and I have checked: the deposit was never once at risk. In that time they have renewed the important contracts monthly — the tea made without asking, the lifts given without sighing, the thermostat war conducted, heroically, without a single shot fired."

One design note for the banner itself: put 480 in the largest type you have. Numbers are the headline at an anniversary — the jokes are the small print, and guests will photograph the big figure and read the small print while they're smiling at it.

My friend group has a tradition: whoever buys a house first hosts New Year. This year it's me — I bought in October. I want to say a few words at midnight, to the friends, in my house, for the first time. Something that marks all three things.

Three threads — the house, the friends, the year — and midnight gives you about ninety seconds before the moment itself. A shape:

"One minute to midnight, so I'll be quick, which is more than the estate agent ever was.

Eleven years this group has done New Year in rented flats, on borrowed sofas, in one memorable kitchen with no chairs. Tonight you're in my house — which means, by the ancient law of this group, that it's partly yours. The spare key has already been discussed. There will be a rota.

I bought four walls and a roof, but I want to say the unfashionable thing out loud: the walls were the easy part to get. What took eleven years was the people in this room — the ones who helped me move, who lent me deposit money I have now repaid, and who have been saying 'your place next year' like a promise until it came true.

So: to the house, to the group, and to next year. Happy New Year — you're home."

"You're home" as the last line does triple duty — to the house, to the friends, to the year ahead — and landing it exactly at midnight makes it the sentence the whole group will repeat at future New Years. Practice the timing once with a clock; a midnight speech that ends at 12:04 has missed its own occasion.

My mother-in-law, Beatriz, turns 70. She came to this country at 30 with two suitcases, built a tailoring business, and put three kids through university. My wife wants me — the in-law — to give the toast, which feels like an honour and a trap. Help me get it right.

The in-law's toast works when it testifies from the unique seat only you occupy: the person who joined later and saw the legend from outside. A shape:

"I am the newest person at this table, so I get to say the thing the family is too used to seeing. When I first met Beatriz, I met a woman who ran a tailoring shop. It took me years to understand I was actually looking at an engine.

She arrived in this country at thirty with two suitcases. Within them, apparently, were: one trade, three children's university educations, a business that dressed half this town's weddings, and a standard of stitching that her competitors still talk about in the tone people use for weather events.

Every family has a person the whole structure rests on, and the structure rarely says so out loud, because the person would wave it away. Beatriz, I am an in-law; I am not bound by the family rule of waving it away.

Seventy years. Two suitcases. Look what was in them. Happy birthday."

"Look what was in them" lets the room complete the tribute themselves — the business, the degrees, the grandchildren at the table — which is more powerful than any list you could recite. As the in-law, your outsider's awe is the one thing nobody else at the table can supply; blood relatives give history, you give witness, and witness is what a 70th is for.

We adopted our dog Biscuit a year ago from the shelter and my partner wants a little 'gotcha day' celebration with the neighbours who helped us settle him. I know it's silly. I want a tiny speech anyway. Embrace the silly.

Silly, done with total commitment, becomes ceremony — that's the whole secret of a gotcha day. Two minutes, deadpan:

"Friends, neighbours, fellow residents of Biscuit's street: we are gathered to mark one year since a four-year-old dog with a crooked ear and no forwarding address moved in and restructured our entire lives.

In twelve months he has: eaten one shoe (the left, always the left), learnt seventeen commands and chosen to obey eleven of them, and become the only member of this household who greets every single one of you at the fence like you've been away for years. Especially you, Mrs Chen — the chicken helped, and we know it.

To the neighbours who walked him when we had the flu, who returned him the two times the gate was left open, and who have never once complained about the barking at the postman, who deserves it: thank you.

To Biscuit: you were a stray with a file that said 'nervous.' Look at you now. You've got people. Happy gotcha day."

The trick is to keep the structure of a real anniversary speech — review of the year, thanks to the community, toast to the guest — because the formality is the joke and the joke is also genuinely the feeling. End by giving him the treat mid-toast; a dog's applause management is different from a human's.

I'm speaking at my father's second wedding. He's 68, marrying Helen, a widow of 71. I'm happy for him but it's complicated — Mum died four years ago and some family members are uneasy. I want words that welcome Helen and honour Mum without making it a memorial. Delicate. Help.

Delicate, and doable — the architecture is: Mum gets one honoured sentence, Helen gets the speech. Like this:

"When Dad told me he was getting married again, he said it the way he'd announce a dentist appointment, and then he looked at me to check whether it was all right. It is all right. It's better than all right, and I want to say why, properly.

Our family knows what a good marriage looks like, because we watched one for forty-three years. Mum is part of why this room knows how to love people well, and she is part of today — not as a shadow over it, but as the reason we recognise the real thing when it shows up again.

And it has shown up. Helen, you make my father laugh in a register I hadn't heard in four years. You have learnt how he takes his tea, how to beat him at cards, and how to get him to a doctor, three skills of escalating difficulty. You have not tried to replace anyone. You have simply, bravely, at seventy-one, started something new, and let us watch a good man come back to full brightness.

Dad, Helen: love is not a finite resource in this family. We checked. There's plenty. To you both."

"Love is not a finite resource — we checked" gives the uneasy relatives a sentence they can hold; it answers the loyalty fear without naming it. Put Mum's sentence early and make it complete in itself, then never look back — a speech that keeps returning to the first marriage turns the second into a footnote, and Helen deserves her own toast, whole.
My workmate Fatima just got engaged and we're doing a little toast in the office kitchen at lunch. I barely know her fiancé's name — it's Yusuf. Keep it short and sweet and office-appropriate.

Office kitchen rules: one minute, no stories that need HR context, and learn the fiancé's name — which you've now got. Try this:

"Everyone, glasses and mugs up. Fatima has news that is better than the quarterly figures: she's engaged, to Yusuf, who by all accounts proposed properly and has been approved by everyone who matters, including, I understand, her grandmother, which is the real examination.

Fatima is the person who remembers everyone's birthday in this office and pretends the calendar does it. So it is officially our turn: we are very happy for you, we expect cake-based updates as plans develop, and we have already started a list of song requests for the wedding DJ, which you may veto exactly once.

To Fatima and Yusuf — congratulations. Mug up."

The grandmother line works in almost any office because it compliments the fiancé without you having to fake knowledge of him. And the song-request joke gives colleagues a harmless way to stay involved in the wedding for months, which is what office celebrations actually are: a long, low-level group hug.

I'm organising a surprise 60th for my husband and I've got to give the speech — the surprise is the party, but the speech is mine and he hates being the centre of attention. There will be about 40 people including his work colleagues and his mother. I want it warm, funny, and survivable for him.

For a man who hates the spotlight, the technique is to keep distributing the attention — to the room, to the years, to other people — and only land it on him in short bursts. A shape:

"For anyone wondering: yes, this was a surprise, and yes, I have checked, he has forgiven me, provisionally.

Sixty years of David. I could do the biography, but you all own pieces of it: his mother owns the early years and several stories I am contractually barred from telling; his colleagues own the version of him that answers email at midnight; his friends own the fishing years, the five-a-side years, and the incident with the tent that is still, legally, under review.

I own the middle of the night version — the one who got up with babies, who held this family steady through two redundancies and his father's death, who still makes me laugh in the supermarket, which is where marriages are actually tested.

David, you hate this, so I'll finish. You are the least self-important person I know and the most important person in this room. Both things. Happy birthday."

"Both things" is the closing trick — it lets him accept the compliment by way of the tease, which is the only door shy men walk through. Keep the whole thing under three minutes and seat him with a drink already in hand; a man who hates attention survives a toast far better holding something.

A former student of mine — I taught her English at secondary school — has just published her first novel and invited me to the launch. She's asked me to say a few words, as her old teacher. I don't want to make it about me or sound like a school report. She was a quiet kid who wrote extraordinary essays in the back of her exercise books.

The teacher's launch speech should be mostly witness: you saw it first, and that's the whole of your claim. A shape:

"I am not going to tell you about teaching Amara, because the truth is she was mostly teaching herself, in the back of her exercise books, while I was at the front explaining the lesson to everyone else.

I would set an essay and hers would arrive with the required two pages — and then, on the last pages of the book, in smaller writing, the real thing: stories, beginnings, whole worlds she hadn't been asked for. I used to read those pages standing by the staffroom kettle and forget my tea.

Teachers are not supposed to have favourites, so I will put it in the professionally approved way: some students you mark. Amara, I read.

This novel is those back pages, grown up and bound. The quiet girl at the back of the class was never being quiet. She was working.

Amara — the kettle's on you now. Congratulations."

"Some students you mark; Amara, I read" is the line that will be quoted back to you both for years, because it converts your professional role into the compliment itself. Keep any school anecdote to the exercise books — one true image is worth more than a career summary, and it hands the evening back to the author, where it belongs.

Our street is holding a memorial tree planting for Mr Abernathy, who lived here 50 years and died in the spring. I've been asked to say a few words at the planting — neighbours, his daughter is coming. Short, outdoors, not religious. Help me.

Outdoors and brief, with the tree doing the long-term talking. Something like this:

"Thank you all for coming, and thank you, Susan, for letting the street do this.

Fifty years Mr Abernathy lived at number nine. He was not a man for speeches — he was a man for holding the ladder, for taking in parcels, for knowing whose car that was and whether it should be there. A street runs on people like that and mostly forgets to say so while they're here. We're saying it now, in the way he'd have preferred: by doing something useful.

This is a rowan. It will have berries for the birds by autumn, and in fifty years — his span on this street — it will be the biggest thing on the green. Children who aren't born yet will know it as just 'the tree.' We will know whose it is.

Susan, the first spadeful is yours."

The rowan details matter: naming what the tree will do (berries, shade, outlasting everyone present) turns a planting into a promise the street can check on yearly. Handing the first spadeful to his daughter closes the words and starts the act — at outdoor ceremonies, the speech should end by beginning the thing itself, not by trailing into applause.
My flatmate just ran her first marathon and I want to say a few words when she gets home Sunday — there'll be a little banner and everything. Short and proud, please.

Short, loud, and mostly cheering — a marathon homecoming is a pep talk, not a speech. Try this when she comes through the door:

"She's home! For those keeping score: twenty-six point two miles, one medal, zero toenails sacrificed — we checked — and a time she will now tell you about in detail for the rest of the year, and we will listen, because she earned it.

Priya, you trained through the winter, in the dark, in the rain, on the mornings when this flat was warm and the sofa was right there. Every one of those mornings was the marathon, really. Today was just the lap of honour.

Sit down. Feet up. The banner is crooked because we were excited. We're proud of you — eat everything."

"Every one of those mornings was the marathon" is the sentence she'll keep, because runners know the race is the receipt, not the purchase. Keep the whole welcome under a minute — she's exhausted, she's emotional, and there is food; the kindest speeches at a finish line are short ones with eating immediately after.

My sister is opening her own bakery next week after years of working for other people. There's a small opening event and she's asked me to say a few words. I want to capture what a risk this is for her and how long she's wanted it, without making it sound scary in front of customers.

Frame the risk as patience, not danger — customers hear "brave" as inspiring and "risk" as worrying. A shape:

"Most people here know Jess as the one who brings the good bread to everything. What you might not know is the timeline. She has wanted this shop since she was nineteen and working the early shift at someone else's bakery, doing her own experiments at midnight in a flat kitchen with a oven that ran twenty degrees hot, which she compensated for by instinct and swearing.

For eleven years she worked for other people and saved. Every payslip had a line in it that nobody saw: this much for the future shop. The future shop now has a name over the door and, I can confirm, an oven that tells the truth.

Jess didn't leap. She built a bridge, one shift at a time, and then she walked over it. This bakery is what patience looks like when it finally gets premises.

Eat something. That's an order from the family. Jess — it's open. It's yours."

"She didn't leap; she built a bridge" reframes a decade of caution as the achievement itself, which is both true and exactly what a nervous founder needs said in public on day one. End by sending people to the counter — an opening speech that finishes by creating a queue has done its commercial job too.

My grandfather is turning 100. The care home is hosting, the local paper might come, and I've been asked to give the family's words. He was a railway signalman, sharp as anything, deaf in one ear. I want something worthy but not a lecture on history.

For a centenary, the century is the backdrop — he is the subject. A shape:

"One hundred years ago, this man was born in a house with no electricity. He has since watched the world invent the television, the jet engine, the internet, and the self-checkout, about which he has opinions he will share at length.

For forty years he was a signalman. He has always said it was a simple job: you are responsible for making sure two trains are never in the same place at the same time, and you must never, ever be wrong. He never was. There are families across this county who never knew his name and owed him their Christmas dinners getting home.

He is deaf in one ear — the left — so if you speak to him today, use the right, and don't waste it on small talk. He likes news, scores, and gossip, in that order.

Grandad: a hundred years, and the signals are all green. Happy birthday."

"The signals are all green" gives him his own trade as the blessing, which a signalman will feel in his bones in a way no generic phrase could reach. If the paper does come, that line is the quote they'll print — trade-specific closings travel. Speak toward his right side, slowly; delivery is part of the gift at 100.

I'm maid of honour for my cousin Lily. She's marrying Ben, whom she met when he was the paramedic who treated her after she fainted at a fun run. I want to use that story in my toast without making light of her fainting — it was scary at the time, she's fine now.

The story is a gift — fate with a uniform — as long as the scare gets one honest beat before the comedy. A shape:

"For anyone who doesn't know how this started: Lily fainted at mile three of a charity fun run, in front of several hundred people, in a tutu. The paramedic who caught her — literally caught her — was Ben.

I was there, and for about a minute it wasn't funny at all. And then this calm voice said, 'You're all right, I've got you,' and did the tests, and made her laugh while her blood pressure was still deciding what to do. I watched my cousin, flat on her back in a tutu, look up at this man and think — I could see her think it — oh. There you are.

She recovered fully, I should say, partly from the faint and partly never.

Ben, you have been catching her ever since: bad days, bad news, one memorable kitchen fire. Lily — he's got you. He's had you since mile three. To Lily and Ben."

"Recovered fully from the faint, and partly never" is the pivot line — it acknowledges the scare and converts it into the romance in a single breath. Check with Lily beforehand that the tutu detail is fair game; a bride's own embarrassing detail is gold when she's consented and lead when she hasn't.

I'm giving the toast at my parents' 60th — diamond — anniversary. I'm the youngest of five. My parents are both 84, still in their own home, still sharp. The family is big and sentimental and there will be tears no matter what. I want to say something that isn't just 'they're wonderful' sixty different ways.

Sixty years needs an argument, not adjectives. Give the room a thesis about what the marriage actually was. A shape:

"Sixty years. I've been asked to say something, and as the youngest of five I have the least authority here, so I did research: I asked each of my siblings what the secret was. I got five different answers, including 'separate televisions' and 'your mother is always right,' and I have concluded there is no secret. There is a practice.

Here is the practice, as observed from the cheap seats of this family for forty years. They repair things immediately — not just objects. A bad evening gets repaired before bed, clumsily sometimes, but before bed. They keep separate interests and a joint calendar. They laugh at the same three jokes they have laughed at since approximately 1974, with undiminished commitment.

And they have buried parents, a sibling, and two of their oldest friends, and they did those years the way they did the good ones: together, in the same direction, at the same pace.

Sixty years is not a long time to be lucky. It's a long time to be consistent. Mum, Dad — the five of us are the evidence, and we're all here, and we all still come home for tea. That's the verdict."

"We're the evidence" is the youngest child's perfect closing — it makes the whole room of descendants into the proof, so the applause lands on the parents from everyone at once. If tears are coming anyway, this structure lets them arrive at the verdict line, which is where you want them: at the end, earned.
My neighbour just had twins and I barely know them — we've only waved over the fence. I want to drop a card round with some words that are warm but not over-familiar. What do I write?

For fence-wave neighbours, the card should be warm, brief, and offer something concrete and low-pressure. Like this:

"Welcome to the world, both of you — and congratulations to the grown-ups.

We're the house at number 14, the ones with the loud hedge trimmer, sorry in advance. Twins is wonderful and also, we gather, a lot. So, two standing offers, no expiry date and no need to reply to this card: if you ever need a parcel taken in, a bin brought back, or just an adult conversation over the fence that isn't about sleep, knock.

And when people ask 'are they identical?' for the four hundredth time, you're allowed to come and hide in our garden.

With love from number 14 — Sarah and Tom."

The offers are calibrated: parcel, bins, fence chat — help that costs the givers little and never requires entering the house, which is exactly the right altitude for new neighbours. The identical-twins joke shows you understand their next year without presuming intimacy. Sign with house number and names; new parents receive forty cards addressed to the babies and remember the one that told them who lives at number 14.

My friend group is scattered across four countries now. Our friend Nadia is getting married in Lisbon and only some of us can go. The rest of us want to record a video toast that doesn't feel like a consolation prize. There are five of us recording from different places.

Make the distance the material instead of the apology — a video that leans into the time zones becomes charming instead of second-best. A script shape:

"[Each person films one section, holding the same object — agree one: a mug.]

Person 1 (morning, Sydney): Nadia, this toast is travelling further than you are. It starts here, where it's already tomorrow.

Person 2 (London): It passes through London, where I am holding the mug we stole from the university kitchen in 2016. It has seen things. So have we.

Person 3 (Toronto): It crosses the Atlantic with a fact: the four of us who can't be there have synchronized our watches, and at the exact moment of your first dance we will all be awake, wherever we are, embarrassing ourselves in our own kitchens.

Person 4 (Lisbon, in person, holding the real mug): And it arrives here. Nadia — the group chat is eight years old and has survived four countries, two career changes and one infamous voice note. A wedding is easy. We are all, in every time zone, at this wedding.

All: To Nadia and Miguel."

The travelling-mug device gives five separate clips one spine, so the edit feels like a relay rather than five apologies stitched together. Film vertically, keep each section under twenty seconds, and have the in-person friend play it on a laptop held high — lo-fi is the aesthetic; a slick production would feel colder.

My dad retired from the fire service last month after 30 years. The station did their thing, but our family wants to mark it at home too — a dinner, and my mum wants me to say words. He's not a speeches man. What's right for the home version?

The home version should be smaller and truer than the station version — less about the service, more about what it cost and gave the family. Like this:

"The station did the official farewell, so this is the unofficial one, and it's shorter, because Dad's already heard one speech this month and his face did something.

Thirty years of shifts. From the family's side of it, that meant: a dad who sometimes slept through Christmas morning because he'd been out all night, who could sleep through anything except a phone ringing in a certain way, and who missed things — matches, plays, one anniversary, sorry Mum — and never once pretended the job hadn't taken them.

But it also meant growing up with a man who ran toward the thing everyone else was running from, and treated it as ordinary. That's a strange and excellent thing to have in your house as a kid. It recalibrates what you think a problem is.

Dad: the phone won't ring that way again. Sleep through Christmas if you like. You've earned the whole morning."

"Sleep through Christmas if you like" reframes the family's old sacrifice as his retirement gift, which lets the room laugh and feel it at the same time. Keep it under two minutes; a man who's endured one official speech this month deserves the home one to be a model of mercy.

I'm the head teacher retiring... no wait, I'm a pupil — I'm 18, leaving school, and I've been asked to speak at the leavers' assembly as head girl. I want to thank the teachers without the usual 'you've been like parents to us' stuff, and say something true to the younger pupils too.

Two audiences, two jobs: honesty for the teachers, a usable gift for the younger pupils. A shape:

"I'm supposed to say the teachers have been like parents to us, but that undersells both parties, so instead: thank you for being professionals. For marking the work at midnight. For the teacher who stayed calm when our chemistry coursework caught actual fire. For the ones who knew which of us needed pushing and which of us needed, that week, to simply be left in peace — and got it right almost every time, which for a building of nine hundred teenagers is statistically absurd.

To the younger years, one piece of intelligence from the front line: the teachers are not the obstacle course. They're the map. The pupils who do best here aren't the cleverest — they're the ones who ask the map questions early instead of at the end, in a panic, in May.

We arrived here at eleven years old with bags bigger than us. We leave with results, references, and strong opinions about the canteen. That's the school's doing and ours.

Thank you. Year 7 — ask the map."

The map metaphor gives the younger pupils an image they'll actually reuse, which is the difference between a leavers' speech that's applauded and one that's remembered in September. Keep the fire anecdote only if it really happened at your school — swap in your building's own legend; every school has exactly one, and naming it gets the biggest reaction of the assembly.
My cousin just qualified as a nurse. Family barbecue this weekend to celebrate. I'm on toast duty apparently. Something short, proud, and a bit funny — she's worked nights through her whole training.

Short and celebratory, with the night shifts as the badge of honour:

"To Aisha: qualified nurse, as of this week, after three years of night shifts, exams taken on no sleep, and learning to find a vein in the dark, which is a party trick she is no longer allowed to demonstrate at family events.

She chose the job nobody in this family was brave enough to choose. When the rest of us are asleep, she's the one awake, being calm at people. That's not a career, that's a public service with better shoes.

Aisha — we're proud of you, we're slightly afraid of your new knowledge of our blood pressures, and we will now be calling you about every rash, forever, and you have only yourself to blame.

To Nurse Aisha."

The closing threat — a lifetime of family rash consultations — is the affectionate tax every newly qualified medic pays at a family barbecue, and delivering it as a toast makes it official. Keep it to a minute; barbecues are standing-up events and the burgers are on a clock.

I need words for my wife's 50th birthday. We've been together since we were 19. She is an extraordinary person — a surgeon — but what I love most is ordinary stuff. I don't want to list her achievements; her colleagues do that. I want the husband's version, and I want it to be good.

The husband's version is the domestic archive — the things only the person who shares the ordinary days can testify to. A shape:

"I have known Helen for thirty-one years, which means I have evidence the rest of you don't. Her colleagues will tell you about the surgeon. I am here to give evidence about the woman who sings, incorrectly and at full volume, to the radio in traffic. Who cannot watch the news without arguing with it. Who has kept, for nineteen years, a list on the fridge of things she intends to fix in this house, and has fixed two of them.

Here's what thirty-one years teaches you. The extraordinary things — the career, the courage, the competence — those are real, and they're the least of it. The thing that actually makes a life is that after the worst days, the ones I can't describe at a birthday, she would still come home and ask about mine like it mattered, and make it matter by asking.

Fifty years old and she still laughs first and loudest at her own jokes, which the rest of us then have to catch up with.

Helen: I met you at nineteen and I have been, in the technical sense, showing off about it ever since. Happy birthday."

"Showing off about it ever since" reframes a lifetime of pride as the husband's happy vanity — it flatters her while keeping the speech about your luck, which is the correct emotional geometry for a spouse's toast. Deliver the fridge list slowly; domestic details need air around them to land.

Our local library was saved from closure by a community campaign and reopens Saturday. I was one of the campaigners. They've asked me to say a few words at the reopening. Keep it joyful, not political — the fight's over, we won.

Victory speeches should be generous — celebrate the place, thank the army, spare the defeated. A shape:

"Eighteen months ago this building had a closure notice in the window, and the most borrowed item in it was the pen we used to sign the petition.

Look at it now. Four thousand signatures. A fundraiser quiz that got so competitive the council sent an observer. A read-in on the steps in February, in the rain, attended by ninety people and one dog in a coat, all reading at the weather.

I don't want to spend today on how close we came. I want to say what this place is, now that it's ours to keep: it's the warmest public room in this town. It's where the toddlers learn the songs, where the students revise, where the newspapers get read by the people who've always read them here, in the same chairs.

Libraries are not closed because nobody loves them. They're saved because somebody says so, out loud, in February, in the rain. You did. It's open. Go and borrow something."

Ending with an instruction — "go and borrow something" — turns the crowd from an audience back into users, which is the campaign's whole point, achieved in one line. Thank the dog in the coat if he attends; a reopening crowd rewards callbacks to the campaign's own folklore more than any civic grandeur.

My older sister has just been ordained as a priest. The family is a mix of churchgoers and cheerful sceptics. I'm saying a few words at the celebration lunch. I want to honour her calling without preaching at the sceptics or making it sound like a job promotion.

The bridge is her character, which both halves of the family know equally well. A shape:

"For those who know Ruth, the news that she has been ordained will have landed the way it landed in our family: as the least surprising surprise of the decade.

She was doing the job unofficially by fourteen. She was the one who sat with people. The friend in crisis, the neighbour in hospital, the cousin whose life had come apart at 2 a.m. — the family has always run an unofficial rota, and Ruth was always on it.
