Whatever your own beliefs — and this table has the full range, and she loves you all and will argue with most of you — you know this about her: when she says she will pray for you, she has already been doing it for years, and when she says she'll be there, she is, with soup.

The church has simply made official what this family has known since she was fourteen. Ruth: we are proud of you. The rota is finally getting paid. Sort of."

"The rota is finally getting paid, sort of" gives the sceptics their laugh and the believers their dignity in the same breath, because the joke is about stipends, not faith. Anchoring the calling in observable behaviour — the sitting-with, the soup — lets everyone at the table verify the tribute from their own experience, whatever they believe about its source.

My twins are starting school in September and our family is doing a little 'night before' tea with the grandparents. I want to say a few words to mark it — they're five, so it's mostly for the adults, but the kids will be there, probably climbing something.

Five-year-olds present means: short, bright, and at least one line aimed directly at them. A shape:

"Right — quick words before the cake, while at least one twin is on the floor and not on the furniture. Tomorrow, these two start school. They have new shoes, new bags, strong opinions about both, and a packed lunch policy they negotiated like trade unionists.

To the grandparents: thank you for the thousand hours that got them here — the reading, the park, the emergency Tuesdays. School doesn't replace any of that. It just adds witnesses.

And to Esme and Noah, the important part: school is where you find out what you're good at and who your people are. You've been practising both for five years. You're ready.

Tomorrow we walk them to the gate. Tonight — cake."

"It just adds witnesses" is the line for the grandparents — it reassures them their role continues rather than concluding, which is the unspoken anxiety at every night-before-school tea. Keep it under two minutes and expect to be interrupted by climbing; a speech that survives a five-year-old's interruption gracefully earns more love than a polished one.

My boss is leaving after eight years and there's a card going round the office. I want to write something in it that's better than 'good luck in your new role!!' — she actually was a good boss. She backed me when a project failed two years ago.

Cards are read in private and kept in drawers — write the sentence she'll re-read. Like this:

"Everyone writes 'good luck' in these cards, so instead, the record: two years ago, when the Henderson project went wrong, you stood in front of the directors and described it as a team misjudgement, in a room where naming me would have been easier and more accurate. I have never forgotten it, and it changed how I try to manage people myself.

That's what a good boss actually is — not the away-days, the cover. You provided it, consistently, for eight years, to the whole team.

Your new company is getting more than it knows. Thank you. — Dan"

One remembered act of protection outweighs a page of adjectives, because she'll recognise the meeting instantly and know the card is evidence, not filler. Sign with your full name, not just initials — leaving cards get kept, and in five years she'll want to know which Dan it was who remembered.

Our amateur football team — Sunday league, we've played together 12 years — is having an end-of-an-era dinner because half the team is retiring from playing. I'm the captain. I want a speech that honours the 12 years without sounding like we're all dying.

The register is valedictory but alive: it's a team talk, not a memorial. A shape:

"Twelve years. When this team started, we had hair, knees, and a combined age that didn't need its own postcode. We have lost all three, in roughly that order.

But let me do the honours properly. Two hundred and something Sunday mornings. Through the era of the waterlogged pitch, the era of Kev's van, the season we won the division's most prestigious award: most improved, which is what they give you when the only direction was up.

Half of us are hanging up our boots, and I want it understood: nobody is leaving this team. The fixture list is changing, not the membership. There will be a five-a-side that some of us can survive, a group chat that will outlive us all, and a standing reservation at this pub.

To the retiring legends: you were the spine. To the rest of us: we are now the spine, God help the team.

Lads — twelve years. Same time next week, different footwear."

"The fixture list is changing, not the membership" is the sentence that does the emotional work — it promises continuity in the language of the thing itself. Sports-team farewells fail when they import funeral grammar; keep every image inside the game (boots, spines, fixtures) and the room stays in the world it loves.

My friend just defended her PhD thesis successfully after six years. We're having drinks tonight. I want a toast that respects how hard it actually was — she nearly quit in year four — without dwelling on the misery.

Honour the hard middle in one clause, then celebrate the ending. A shape:

"To Dr Osei — and I will be using the title at full volume for the foreseeable future, including in supermarkets.

Six years. A thesis that changed direction twice, a supervisor who retired mid-project, and a fourth year that we do not describe in detail except to say: she stayed. That's the whole story of a doctorate, really. It's not a test of brilliance. Brilliance is common. It's a test of staying — of opening the document on the thousandth morning.

Today a room of experts asked her the hardest questions in her field and she answered them standing in her own work like she owned it. Because she does.

Amma: you stayed, and then you finished, and those are different achievements and you did both. Dr Osei, everybody."

"She stayed" does more honour than any praise of talent, because everyone who has done a long hard thing knows the talent was never the scarce resource. Name the year-four crisis only as "she stayed" — the room that knows will feel it, and the room that doesn't will simply hear resolve. First use of the new title should be yours, early and loud: it never stops being a thrill for about a year, so be generous with it all evening.

I'm giving the eulogy for my father-in-law. I only knew him for the last nine years of his life — he was a quiet, gruff Yorkshireman who ran an allotment and distrusted speeches. His sons are too upset to speak. I want to honour him as the man I actually knew, not pretend I knew him from childhood.

Speaking as the late arrival is honest, and honesty is your licence. A shape:

"I only had nine years of Arthur, and he would want me to start by admitting that, because he distrusted anyone claiming more than they knew — about tomatoes, about weather, about people.

What I knew was this. A man who said perhaps forty words at a family lunch and meant every one of them. A man whose allotment fed, by my count, eleven households, delivered in bags left on doorsteps without a note, as if vegetables simply occurred. A man who, when my daughter was born, held her for exactly one photograph and then said, 'She'll do,' which from Arthur was a five-star review and which we have quoted weekly since.

His sons could tell you about the first sixty years. I can only testify to the last nine, and my testimony is: the gruffness was a fence, and inside the fence was one of the most generous gardens I have ever known a person to keep. In every sense.

Arthur: she did do. We all did, because of you. Rest now. The allotment rota is sorted — he'd want that confirmed."

The closing line about the rota answers the only question a practical man would ask of his own funeral, and it will make the family laugh through tears, which is the sound he would have wanted. Naming the limits of your knowledge at the start buys you the room's trust for everything after — mourners forgive an in-law anything except pretending.

My younger sister just bought her first car with her own money after saving for two years. Family lunch Sunday. I want a little toast — it's not a huge life event but she worked hard for it and I want her to feel celebrated.

Small milestones deserve exact-sized toasts — sixty seconds, full warmth. Try this:

"To Beth, and to the car, which I have inspected and which has four wheels and, importantly, a working horn.

Two years she saved for this. Two years of skipped takeaways, extra shifts, and a savings account she checked like weather. Nobody gave her this car. There is no bank of mum and dad in this story, no scratch card. She earned it in the least glamorous way possible: repeatedly, on purpose, over two years.

That car is not transport. It's a certificate she issued herself.

Beth: drive safe, come home often, and remember that as the family member with a car you are now legally a taxi. To Beth."

The taxi joke at the end converts the family's pride into the family's demands, which is how siblings actually express love. And "a certificate she issued herself" gives the toast one sentence with weight — a small occasion needs exactly one, no more, or it tips into parody.

My colleague and friend Yusuf is taking early retirement at 58 to look after his wife, who has MS. The office farewell is next week and I'm speaking. I want to honour both his work and his reason for leaving, without pity — his wife Amina would hate pity and so would he.

No pity — the register is respect for a decision made from strength. A shape:

"Yusuf has run the numbers on this, because Yusuf runs the numbers on everything, so let me give you his: thirty-one years in this department. Four systems migrated. Two generations of staff trained, including me, including, I suspect, some people in this room who still call him when the spreadsheet does something frightening.

He is leaving at fifty-eight, earlier than planned, and I want to say this in the plain terms he'd insist on: he has looked at what matters most and reallocated his time accordingly. It is the most Yusuf decision imaginable. The rest of us talk about priorities. He has just filed his, in action.

Amina gets, from next month, the full-time services of the most competent person I know. This department's loss is extremely well spent.

Yusuf: the spreadsheets will fear no one now. Go well. We'll hold the standard you set, or at least we'll hold the manual you wrote, which amounts to the same thing."

"He has filed his priorities, in action" honours the reason without a drop of pity, because it frames caregiving as allocation — his own professional language, which dignifies rather than softens it. Avoid all words like "brave" and "sadly"; men like Yusuf experience them as demotions. Competence praised, decision respected, door left open: that's the whole job.

My grandma just moved into a new flat near us after living in her old house for 50 years. We're doing a small housewarming tea for her this weekend — just family. I want to say a few words that make the new place feel like a celebration, not a loss.

The key is to toast the new flat's future and let the old house be honoured in a single fond clause. Try this:

"Welcome to the new headquarters. Fifty years in the old house, and Gran ran it like a small country — everyone fed, everyone's business known, borders strictly enforced.

This flat has a lot to live up to, but it has advantages: no stairs between Gran and the kettle, a window over the green, and us, ten minutes away, which she claims is 'just far enough.'

Gran, a house is not the walls. It's the person who makes people take their shoes off and stay for one more cup. You've brought that with you. It's already here. I can tell because I've been here four minutes and I'm on my second biscuit.

To the new headquarters — long may it reign."

"Us, ten minutes away, which she claims is just far enough" gets the laugh and quietly celebrates the move's actual purpose — closeness — without anyone having to say the word "downsizing" or look sad. At a move like this, the family's job is to be visibly pleased in the new rooms; your toast sets that weather for the whole tea.

I'm speaking at the wedding of two friends who are both 45 and marrying for the first time. Everyone's thrilled but there's this undercurrent of 'finally' that I know they hate. I want a toast that treats their timing as right, not late.

Name the timing as design, not delay — one elegant sentence can retire the word "finally" for the whole day. A shape:

"I have been asked not to use the word 'finally,' so I won't. I will say this instead: some people marry the first person they can imagine a life with. Kate and Daniel waited until they found the person they couldn't imagine the alternative to. Those are different sports.

They bring to this marriage something the young are still collecting: two complete lives. Two careers, two sets of friends who are now, by law, one set. Two households of furniture, which has caused a diplomatic incident the couple is handling with a spreadsheet. And a total absence of illusion, which turns out to be the most romantic thing in this room. They have seen each other tired, ill, grieving, and badly dressed, in advance. They chose anyway, with the evidence in.

That is not a late start. That is a marriage beginning at full strength.

Kate, Daniel: to the evidence, and to you."

"A marriage beginning at full strength" is the reframing the couple will quote for years — it converts the room's pity into envy, which is where it should be. The furniture spreadsheet joke matters too: it proves their union is practical and negotiated, a grown-up artefact, and the room laughs in recognition of its own compromises.

My son is 21 next week. He's at university, coming home for a family meal. I want to say something at 21 that isn't the usual 'keys to the door' stuff — he's a thoughtful kid, a bit anxious about the future, and I want the words to actually steady him.

For an anxious 21-year-old, the gift is a realistic map, not a pep talk. A shape:

"Twenty-one. The speeches for this birthday usually hand over keys and declare you an adult, so instead, some field notes from further down the road you're worried about.

The twenties are not a race with a visible start line. They are a decade of trying on lives, most of which won't fit, and that is not failure — that's the fitting process. The friends who matter will not be counting your milestones. Neither, despite appearances, is anyone else.

Here's what I know about you at twenty-one: you are kind under pressure, you finish what you start even when it stops being interesting, and you ring your grandmother without being asked. Those three things will carry you further than any five-year plan.

You don't have to know. You have to keep going and stay kind. The knowing catches up.

Happy birthday, Tom. We're in your corner at every distance."

"The knowing catches up" is the sentence an anxious graduate-age kid will actually store — it separates effort (his job) from clarity (which arrives on its own schedule). Avoid all comparisons with siblings, cousins, or your own timeline; a 21st toast should narrow the world to the birthday person and the people at the table who are in his corner.

I'm the executor and oldest friend of a man who died leaving no close family — just friends. His name was Colin, he was a postman for 40 years and a chess player. The funeral is small, maybe 20 people, all friends. As the one organising it, I feel I should speak, but what do you say when friends are the family?

You say exactly that — friends as family is the theme, and a chosen family deserves its own grammar. A draft:

"Colin had no family in the way the forms mean it, so the forms would look at this room and see twenty friends. I want to correct the record before we begin: this is his family. It is simply the kind you assemble.

He assembled it the way he did everything: on his rounds and over a chess board. Forty years a postman — he knew every dog, every gate, every household's news before the household did, and he carried all of it with a discretion the secret services could study. Over the board he was merciless and magnificent, and he taught half this room to play, which means his real legacy is distributed: a bit of Colin now sits in every game any of us plays, forever, usually beating us.

He used to say a chess game is just two people keeping each other company in an organised way. That was his whole life, really. The rounds, the board, the pub quiz team — organised company. He was very, very good at keeping people company.

Colin: the company is here. All of it. Checkmate was never the point, and you knew it."

"Organised company" gives the room a definition of him they can keep — postmen and chess players both deal in faithful, repeated presence, and naming that dignifies a modest life without inflating it. As organiser, keep the practical announcements (wake venue, flowers, the chess-club donation) for after the eulogy, in a separate, lighter voice — mourners need a clean line between the tribute and the logistics.

I'm MC at my sister's wedding — 120 guests, speeches between courses. I don't want rambling introductions. Give me a running order for the speech section with the actual words I use to introduce each speaker, so the whole thing feels like a ceremony rather than a series of interruptions.

Here is a running order with your exact links written out — the MC's job is to make each speaker feel expected:

| Slot | Speaker | Your introduction |
|---|---|---|
| After starters | Father of the bride | "A wedding runs on many things, but it starts with the people who started the bride. Please welcome her father, George." |
| After mains | Best man | "Every groom needs one witness who knows the whole record and agrees to publish only part of it. The best man, Chris." |
| Before dessert | Maid of honour | "The bride's oldest friend has been rehearsing this in her head since they were twelve. It shows. Please welcome Priya." |
| Close | The couple | "Last, the only two people here who haven't been nervous all day about speaking. A few words from the newlyweds." |

Three rules that make this work as ceremony rather than interruption. First, introduce by relationship before name — the room settles when it knows who it's listening to. Second, keep every link under twenty seconds and end each one standing, glass down, looking at the speaker, so the applause has a clean target. Third, never summarise a speech after it ends; a single "thank you" and the next course. The one exception: if a speech runs past seven minutes, catch the speaker's eye and raise your glass slightly — agree this signal with all speakers at the rehearsal, when everyone still likes each other.

My parents are both turning 75 within a month of each other and we're doing one joint party. I want a toast that celebrates them as a pair without it becoming a second anniversary speech — it's their birthdays.

Birthdays as a pair means celebrating two people who happen to share a season, not the marriage itself. A shape:

"This party has two guests of honour, which has caused a seating-plan situation and a cake situation, both resolved by the traditional method: two cakes.

Seventy-five years each. Dad: seventy-five years of mending things that were not, technically, broken, of knowing every shortcut in the county and most of the long cuts too. Mum: seventy-five years of feeding people as a first language, of remembering every birthday in a family of forty, including the in-laws, including the dog.

People will say they come as a pair, and they do — but I want the record to show they're also two of the most individual people I know, who have spent fifty years carefully not sanding each other's edges off.

Two cakes, two candles-counts nobody is attempting, two happy birthdays. Mum, Dad — blow out your own. You've earned separate wishes."

"Separate wishes" is the closing distinction that keeps it a birthday toast rather than an anniversary in disguise — it hands each parent their own moment inside the shared party. Give each parent one solo paragraph before the joint close; symmetry is the whole design, so count the lines and balance them.

My little sister just got her exam results and she's into her first-choice university. We're doing a family tea tonight. Quick proud toast, please — she's worked so hard and had a rough year with illness in the middle of it.

Proud, quick, and let the rough year be honoured in one phrase rather than a paragraph:

"To Maya: first-choice university, confirmed this morning, after a year that included revising from a hospital waiting room and an exam season held together with flashcards and stubbornness.

The grades are excellent. But the family position is that the grades are not the impressive part. The impressive part is that she kept going in a year that gave her every excuse not to, and she never once used the excuse.

Maya: the university thinks it's getting a student. It's getting the flashcards-and-stubbornness method, and it doesn't stand a chance.

Tea's up. She's buying when the student loan lands."

"She never once used the excuse" is the sentence that does the honouring — it acknowledges the illness year without turning a celebration into a medical retrospective. At a results tea, keep the toast to a minute; the evening belongs to relief and food, and long speeches are for occasions with less cake-based urgency.

I'm speaking at my best friend's 40th. He's a single dad of two, works as a paramedic, and is honestly the most selfless person I know. I want the toast to actually embarrass him with how much we all think of him — he's always deflecting.

To toast a deflector, bring witnesses — make the praise a group act he can't wave off alone. A shape:

"Dan has a professional skill he uses on civilians: he deflects compliments the way he deflects everything, calmly and with humour. So the family and I have prepared for this. This toast has been signed by twenty-three people. It's in the card. He cannot deflect a petition.

Exhibit A: the night my car died at 1 a.m. with a baby in the back, and the paramedic who arrived off-duty, in his own car, because I'd rung him instead of the breakdown line and he'd simply come. Exhibit B: two kids who think their dad hung the moon, who are, on the evidence, correct. Exhibit C: a street's worth of neighbours whose emergencies have a habit of becoming Dan's evenings.

Forty years of running toward other people's worst days and coming home to be the best part of his kids' ordinary ones.

Dan: the petition is unanimous. You're loved, on the record, no appeals. Happy birthday."

The petition device solves the deflector problem structurally: he can shrug off your opinion but not a signed document from twenty-three people. Read two exhibits only — a third makes it a trial. And have the card physically present; producing it at "it's in the card" gets the laugh and the tear in the same second.

I'm writing the order of service booklet for my grandmother's funeral and I want a short printed tribute on the back page — she was a baker, famous in our family for feeding everyone. About 150 words, something people will keep. Can you draft it and tell me why it works in print?

Here is a printed tribute at keeping-length, followed by why it's built the way it is:

"IN MEMORY OF EDITH HARPER, 1938–2026

Edith fed people. It was her first language and her whole argument. Her kitchen produced bread for neighbours, cakes for every family occasion for sixty years, and a standing rule that nobody left her house hungry or unlistened-to.

She taught three generations of this family that most problems are smaller after tea, and that the rest are at least more bearable.

The recipes are written down. The family has them. What cannot be written down — the timing, the patience, the way she knew — we carry as best we can.

'Nobody leaves this house hungry.' Nobody did."

Why it works in print: it is built from short declarative sentences, because print at a funeral is read through tears and long sentences drown. The quoted rule at the end does the work of a photograph — everyone who ever sat in that kitchen hears her voice saying it, which is the one thing a booklet can give that a speech cannot repeat. Keep it under the photograph if there is one, set it in a larger size than feels necessary, and leave white space around it: on the back of an order of service, space is respect.

My husband and I are adopting a child — a girl, age six, named June. The adoption is finalised next month and we're having a welcome party with family. I want to say words at it that are joyful and careful — she'll be there, and I don't want language about 'saving' her or her being 'lucky.' She's joining a family, that's all.

Your instinct is exactly right, and the language to use is belonging, not rescue. A shape:

"Today is a paperwork day and a party day, and the paperwork is the least interesting part, so I'll be quick.

June: this is your family. Some of them are loud. The man over there is your grandad and he has already bought you a football kit in the wrong size, which is how he shows love. This lady is your auntie and she has been practising your favourite songs, badly, for a month.

Families are not really about who starts them or when. A family is the people who learn how you take your hot chocolate, who know which stair creaks, who show up. We are all learning, and we intend to be excellent at it.

June, you don't have to do anything to belong here. Belonging isn't earned. It's just true, starting today, on the paperwork and in this room.

Cake is next. You get the first slice — that's a family rule we made up just now, and it's permanent."

"Belonging isn't earned — it's just true" is the sentence the whole speech exists to deliver, to June and to any adult in the room carrying rescue language in their heads. The made-up cake rule matters too: new family traditions invented on day one give a six-year-old something that began with her, in a family where most traditions predate her. Keep it short, keep it at her eye level when you reach her name, and let the party do the rest.

I'm best man for my friend Callum. He and his fiancée Megan met at a climbing gym — she was instructing, he was, by his own admission, showing off and fell off the wall in front of her. I want that in the toast, but I also want one genuinely moving line, because underneath the clowning he's the most loyal friend I have.

The structure is: comedy carries the room, then one unguarded sentence lands because everything before it was funny. A shape:

"Callum met Megan at the climbing gym, where she was the instructor and he was a man with a plan. The plan was to impress her on the hard wall. What actually happened is that he fell off the hard wall, in a harness, slowly, like a descending spider, while she held the rope and, to her credit, did not laugh until the safety briefing was complete.

She held the rope that day. I want you to notice the pattern, because it's been the pattern ever since: Callum attempts something slightly beyond him, and Megan is the reason it ends well. The business idea. The marathon. The flat-pack wardrobe that nearly ended a friendship — mine, I was inside it.

Here's the true bit, and then I'll stop. In fifteen years I have never once rung this man and not had him come. Not once. Whatever the hour, whatever the weather, whatever state I was in. He comes.

Megan: he's yours now, and the rope is a shared asset. Callum — she held it first, and she's held it best. To Callum and Megan."

"I have never once rung this man and not had him come" is the moving line, and it works because it's a verifiable fact about loyalty rather than a compliment about personality. Place it at roughly eighty percent through the speech; a best man's toast should exit shortly after its one sincere sentence, while the room is still feeling it.

My mother is being honoured by her old school — she taught there 35 years and they're naming the library after her. There's a ceremony and she's asked me to speak because she says she'll cry if she does. I want to give the school something worthy of her and give her something she can just sit and receive.

Speaking so she can simply receive it is a beautiful brief — the speech should carry her the way she carried the school. A shape:

"My mother asked me to say these words because she said she would cry, so if I cry, the family position is that it's hereditary and she started it.

Thirty-five years in one school. She taught the children of her first pupils, and in two cases — she keeps count, I am not at liberty to say it isn't three — she was on track for the grandchildren. She ran the library like a small republic: everybody equal, everybody welcome, talking permitted at a volume she alone determined, and woe betide anyone who returned a book with a turned-down page.

A library with her name on it is the correct monument, because she never believed knowledge belonged to the clever. She believed it belonged to whoever walked in. Thousands of children walked in.

Mum: the room is yours now, permanently, in brass. You may sit down at last. You've earned the chair by the window."

"The chair by the window" gives the ceremony a final image of rest that a working teacher of 35 years will feel physically. And opening with her instruction — that you'd cry on her behalf — lets the room know any tears are authorised by the guest of honour herself, which frees her to simply sit, receive, and, if she likes, cry anyway.

My wife died two years ago. Our daughter is getting married next month and I'm giving the father-of-the-bride speech. I want to mention her mum — she should be present in the day — but I cannot turn it into a grief speech and I will not be able to hold it together if I dwell. I need something with a light touch that still says it.

This is the hardest balance in wedding speeches, and the craft answer is: one sentence, early, complete — then the day belongs to the living. A shape:

"Before anything else, one sentence, and then we celebrate. Anna's mum, Sarah, would have been insufferable today — proud beyond all reason — and she is here in the way that matters: she's in Anna's laugh, which is her laugh, and anyone who knew Sarah has already heard it twice today. That's the sentence. She'd have wanted the party more than the pause.

Now. Anna. I have watched you grow from a person who cried at a dropped ice cream to a person who organised this entire wedding with a spreadsheet that had colour-coded contingencies for weather. Daniel, a word of advice: marry into the spreadsheet. It's the family firm now.

Daniel, you are welcome in this family in the full sense: you have been given the honest chair at our table, the one where nobody performs. It's the best seat we have.

To Anna and Daniel — and to absent friends, who are, as established, only technically absent."

"Only technically absent" is a closing that returns to her without reopening the grief — it bookends the single sentence and lets you end raised-glass rather than broken. Practise the early sentence aloud, alone, several times before the day; a sentence rehearsed to boredom at home is a sentence you can survive in public. And brief the best man to start the applause hard at the end of it — a room that claps carries a father over the line.

We're a small company, 14 people. Our founder, Grace, is handing over to a new managing director after 20 years and there's a dinner. I've been asked to give the farewell toast as the longest-serving employee after her. I want to honour what she built without it sounding like a corporate press release.

Small companies have real folklore — use it instead of mission language. A shape:

"Twenty years ago this company was Grace, a laptop, and a client she'd persuaded to take a chance. I was employee number two, hired in an interview conducted in a café because there was no office, and paid, for the first month, in a way I'd describe as 'eventually.'

What she built is not really the client list, though it's a good one. It's the rules we still run on, most of which were never written down: answer the phone like a human. Tell the client the bad news first. Never let a junior take the blame for a senior's decision — she took two of mine, in rooms I wasn't in, and I only found out years later.

Grace is handing over a company of fourteen people who would, and I have polled this, follow her into most ventures and several swamps.

Grace: you built the place we all wanted to work. It stays built. To Grace — and the laptop is being retired with full honours."

"Paid in a way I'd describe as eventually" is the kind of founding detail that makes a room of fourteen roar, because they all own a version of it. Corporate language fails at farewells because companies aren't loved; founders' habits are. List her rules, not her achievements, and the toast becomes a constitution the new MD can actually inherit.

My friend is celebrating five years sober and a few of us are having a dinner for him. He said he's okay with it being marked. I want to say a few words that honour the achievement without making it sound like a before-and-after advert or dwelling on the bad years.

Mark the achievement as work, not as a miracle — that's the respectful register. A shape:

"Five years. I want to say this plainly, because plain is how Pete did it: this is one of the hardest things a person can do, and he did it in the least dramatic way imaginable. One day, then another day, then about eighteen hundred more of them, most of them completely ordinary, some of them not.

I'm not going to do the before-and-after speech, because Pete was never a before. He was our friend in the bad years too, and he's our friend now, and the thread never broke — he made sure of that, which, when you think about it, is the most Pete part of the whole story.

What five years looks like from this side of the table: he's the person we ring now. At the start, we rang to check on him. Somewhere in those eighteen hundred days that reversed, and nobody noticed it happening.

Pete: to the days. All of them, counted and counting."

"The thread never broke — he made sure of that" refuses the before/after frame while still honouring the scale of the change, which is exactly the distinction your friend will be listening for. Keep drink-based toast language out of it entirely — raise coffee, raise water, raise nothing but your voice if the table prefers; the words carry it.
My husband just got a promotion he's wanted for years. We're having a little family dinner tonight. I want to say a quick toast that makes him feel seen — he's worked late so many nights for this.

Quick, warm, and let him know the late nights were noticed, not just endured:

"Before we eat: to Daniel, who got the job. The actual job, the one he's been describing at this table for three years, usually while reheating his dinner.

We've all watched the late nights, the laptop at weekends, the phone calls taken in the garden so the kids could be loud in here. I want it said out loud at least once: we saw it, it counted, and it worked.

Daniel — the family is proud of you, the reheating era is officially over, and dinner tonight is hot and on time in your honour, which is the greatest luxury this house can offer.

To Daniel. Eat while it's warm."

"We saw it, it counted, and it worked" is the whole speech in one line — promotions get celebrated for the outcome, but the person who earned one wants the cost witnessed. The reheating joke turns the family's sacrifice into shared comedy rather than a grievance, which is the difference between a toast and a reckoning. Keep it before the food; a promotion toast after dessert competes with tired children and loses.

Our rowing club is celebrating its centenary — founded 1926. I'm club captain and I open the centenary dinner. There will be members from 18 to 90, including descendants of founders. I want opening words that connect the generations without a history lecture.

Connect them through the river and the ritual, which haven't changed, rather than through dates. A shape:

"A hundred years ago, the founders of this club put a boat on this river at six in the morning because there was nowhere else they'd rather be at six in the morning. I can report, as this year's captain, that the reasoning has not improved and neither has the hour.

Look at this room. We have members who rowed here in the sixties and members who joined in September. We have a founder's great-granddaughter at table four, who rows the same stretch of water, past the same boathouse door, swearing at the same bend in the river, which has defeated a century of us impartially.

A rowing club is a machine for turning strangers into crews. It has run for a hundred years on cold mornings, blister tape, and the unshakeable belief that the next outing will be the good one.

To the founders: the boat still goes out. To everyone here: you're the reason. The next hundred starts at six tomorrow — attendance is, as ever, compulsory in spirit."

"Swearing at the same bend" gives every generation in the room a shared, slightly irreverent inheritance, which binds faster than reverence does. Centenary speeches fail by becoming minutes of a meeting held in 1926; keep the past to two sentences and spend the rest on the living room — the descendants came to see their family inside a continuing thing, not a concluded one.

My sister-in-law just became a British citizen — she's from Brazil, been here nine years. We're having a family lunch to celebrate her citizenship ceremony. I want to say a few words that welcome her properly, as family and as a fellow citizen, without being cheesy about flags.

Welcome her in the specific, not the patriotic — belonging is made of small recognised things. A shape:

"Nine years ago Camila arrived with a suitcase, a job offer, and a level of optimism about British weather that has since been corrected by experience.

This week she stood in the town hall and became, officially, what this family has considered her for years. The ceremony gives you a certificate and a photograph with the mayor. What it can't give you is the part you've already earned the slow way: you know which bin goes out on Thursdays. You have opinions about the trains. You make a better cup of tea than anyone born here, and we have stopped pretending otherwise.

Citizenship, in the end, is mostly that: knowing how a place works and deciding it's yours anyway, weather and trains included.

Camila: welcome, again — this time with paperwork. We're proud to share a country and a table with you."

"Welcome, again — this time with paperwork" is the line that frames the ceremony correctly: the family belonging came first, the state is catching up. Avoid flag imagery entirely; for a new citizen, the tea and the bins are the true national symbols, and she'll laugh in recognition because she's earned every one of them.

I'm giving a speech at the memorial service for a beloved local GP, Dr Anand, who served our town for 45 years. Half the town will be there. I was his patient and later his friend. I want to capture what he meant to a whole community without listing his career.

A community doctor is measured in other people's memories — build the speech from the town's evidence, not his CV. A shape:

"There is hardly a family in this town that Dr Anand did not, at some point, sit with in the worst hour of their lives — and a great many of us he also saw in the best ones, because he delivered, by the surgery's own count, over nine hundred of the babies in this valley, some of whom are here today with babies of their own.

He had a gift that cannot be taught in medical school: he remembered. Not just your history — your mother's name, your daughter's exam, the dog. You were never a case. You were a chapter he was following, in a book he intended to finish.

When my father was dying, Dr Anand came to the house on his day off, in his own car, and sat with us in the kitchen after, drinking tea he didn't want, because he understood that the appointment wasn't over when the medicine was.

A town does not replace a man like that. It does something else: it becomes, in small ways, more like him. More patient. More likely to sit a moment longer in someone's kitchen.

Dr Anand: the valley is yours. Rest well."

"It becomes more like him" converts communal grief into a communal instruction, which is the only useful thing a memorial speech can give a town. One personal scene — your father's kitchen — is enough; the room will supply their own nine hundred versions, and a speech that leaves space for the audience's memories is remembered as if it had contained them all.

My two oldest friends are marrying each other — I've known them both since school, separately, and they got together at my 30th birthday party five years ago. I'm giving a joint toast as the person who (accidentally) introduced them. I want to claim my credit tastefully and celebrate them properly.

Claim the credit in the first ten seconds, as a joke, then spend the rest of the speech giving it away. A shape:

"I would like to begin by accepting full responsibility. My thirtieth birthday, my flat, my terrible playlist — and these two spent the whole evening in the kitchen, allegedly washing up, for four hours.

I have known them separately since we were eleven. I watched Emma date a sequence of men best described as cautionary tales. I watched Josh insist, for a decade, that he was 'not the settling type,' usually while fixing something in my flat and staying for dinner. I never once put them together in my head, which tells you everything about my gifts as a matchmaker and is why I am retiring from the profession at the top.

What I see now is obvious: two people who make each other funnier, calmer, and braver, in roughly that rotation. The kitchen of my flat has a plaque now. It's imaginary, but it's there.

Emma, Josh: my work here is done. To you both — and to washing up, the most romantic of the chores."

"Retiring from the profession at the top" closes the credit-claim as comedy before it can curdle into vanity — one joke of ownership, then total generosity. The imaginary plaque is the image to end the middle on: it gives the couple a founding myth located in your friendship, which is the true gift a mutual friend's toast can offer.

My dad is 60 and we're surprising him with a This-Is-Your-Life style evening — old friends, photos, stories. I'm hosting and opening it. I want opening words that set the tone: warm, funny, and clear that this is a celebration, not a roast, even though stories will be told.

An opening for a life-review evening has one job: set the contract between love and laughter. A shape:

"Good evening, and welcome to an event Dad knows nothing about, which for a man who reads the instructions on everything is already a personal crisis.

The format is simple. Tonight we are going to walk through sixty years of this man — the school years, the hair years, the band years, the dad years — with photographs, witnesses, and several stories he has previously paid good money to suppress.

One rule, and I will enforce it as host: tonight is a celebration wearing a roast's coat. We will laugh at him the way you can only laugh at someone the whole room would take a bullet for, metaphorically, and in one case — Uncle Ray — nearly literally, and we'll come to that.

Dad: you are among the people who know you best and love you most, in that order of danger. Sit down. It's your life."

"A celebration wearing a roast's coat" gives the storytellers their licence and their limit in a single phrase — they'll pitch their contributions to match it all evening. And the closing line, "It's your life," said simply, converts the ambush into an honour before the first photograph appears, which matters: a surprised man should hear love before he hears laughter.

I'm organising my parents' ruby wedding — 40 years — and I've been asked to run the evening. Can you give me a structure for the celebration itself: the running order, and the short words I say at each transition? I want it to feel like a ceremony with a spine, not just a party with speeches floating in it.

Here is a spine for the evening, with your transition lines written out — transitions are what make an event feel ceremonial:

| Moment | What happens | Your words |
|---|---|---|
| Arrival | Guests take seats, parents enter last | "Forty years ago these two walked into a room as a new couple. Tonight they walk in as the reason for the room. Please stand for Margaret and David." |
| Before dinner | The toast | "Forty years, two children, one house rebuilt twice, and a marriage conducted largely through the medium of lists. To Margaret and David." |
| Between courses | The slideshow | "What follows is forty years in forty photographs. Parents: heckling is permitted. Denials will be noted and ignored." |
| After dessert | Open floor, three speakers max | "Three people have been granted the floor. Others may apply in writing for the golden wedding." |
| Close | Parents' reply, then music | "The couple have the last word, as they have had, jointly, since 1986. Then dancing, which they also started." |

Three structural choices do the work. The parents enter last and standing, which frames them as the occasion rather than the hosts. Open floor is capped at three speakers and announced as capped — an uncapped floor is how warm evenings die at 11 p.m. And the couple closes: at a ruby wedding the final authority in the room should be the marriage itself, not the organiser. Keep every transition under thirty seconds; the spine should be felt, not noticed.

My grandmother died at 97 — she outlived two husbands, ran a post office for 30 years, and was sharp to the end. I'm giving the eulogy. I don't want it to be sad-sad; she had an enormous life and she'd want the good stories told. Help me write a eulogy with joy in it.

A long life fully lived earns a eulogy with laughter in the front half and tenderness at the end. A draft:

"Ninety-seven years. Gran used to say she wasn't old, she was 'well-established,' and she intended to complain to management if the establishment closed early.

She ran the village post office for thirty years, which means she knew everyone's business in the most literal sense and repeated none of it, which in a village is a form of sainthood. She outlived two husbands and spoke of both with a twinkle that suggested the reviews were favourable. She learned email at eighty-eight to write to her great-grandchildren, and her sign-off, every time, was 'Gran (Mrs E. Whitfield to the bank).'

She was sharp to the end. In her last month she beat the care-home manager at Scrabble, disputed a gas bill from her bed, and won.

Here is the tenderness, and then I'll stop. She used to say a person isn't gone while their stories are still being told at tables. By that measure, look at this room: she is in no danger whatsoever.

Gran: well-established, permanently. The floor is yours, as it always was."

The sign-off detail — "Gran (Mrs E. Whitfield to the bank)" — is the kind of specific that makes a whole funeral smile in recognition; if she had a signature phrase of her own, put it in that slot instead. End by handing her the floor: a woman who ran every room she entered deserves a eulogy that exits on her authority, not on your grief.

My friend just opened a community café after being made redundant last year — she turned it around completely. Opening day is Saturday and she's asked me to say a few words. I want to celebrate the comeback without making the redundancy the headline.

The comeback is the seasoning, not the story — one clause, then all café. A shape:

"A year ago, life handed Nia a redundancy letter. She has since converted it, through a process involving one business plan, forty-seven recipe tests, and a builder called Stan who now has a loyalty card, into this café.

I am not going to dwell on last year, because Nia doesn't, and because look around: this room is the reply. What I will say is that this café already does the thing she always did at her own kitchen table — it notices people. The menu has the soup her neighbour requested during the tests. The corner table is reserved, permanently, for the crossword people, of whom there are apparently many.

A community café isn't opened, exactly. It's adopted, by its street. Street: the adoption papers are on the counter. They're called menus.

Nia: first shift. We're all regulars now."

"This room is the reply" retires the redundancy in four words and turns the opening crowd into the evidence — no one has to hear the hard year narrated. Ending by recruiting the audience as regulars is commercially kind as well as warm: an opening speech that finishes with the room feeling enrolled has done the founder a lasting favour.

I have to speak at the wedding of my daughter to her partner of 12 years. They're in their late 30s, they have a house, a dog, two kids already. Some relatives call it 'about time.' I want my speech to honour the family they already built, not pretend the wedding starts everything.

Then the speech's thesis is: today formalises, it does not begin. A shape:

"I am not going to pretend this wedding is a beginning. I was at the beginning. The beginning was a flat with no heating and a dog that ate the skirting board. This — this is the ceremony catching up with the facts.

The facts are these. For twelve years these two have run a household, raised two children who are currently somewhere in this venue being fed cake by relatives, survived a renovation, a redundancy, and a dog with expensive hobbies. They have done every hard part of marriage already, in the correct order and several incorrect ones.

So what is today for? Today is for saying it out loud, in front of everyone, in good clothes: we chose this, we choose it still, and we want witnesses.

Well. You have them. Some of us have been witnesses since the skirting board.

Sophie, Laura: the paperwork has caught up with the love. It took it twelve years. Congratulations — retroactively, and from here on."

"Congratulations — retroactively" is the line that dissolves the "about time" framing: it treats the twelve years as already-married in substance, which is the couple's own account of their lives. Mentioning the children briefly and comically — fed cake by relatives — places them inside the celebration rather than apologising for their existence at it, which older relatives' speeches sometimes accidentally do.

My brother is a firefighter and he just got a commendation for bravery — he pulled a man from a house fire. There's a family dinner and he is deeply embarrassed by the whole thing. I want to toast him in a way he can actually sit through.

For a man embarrassed by heroism, praise the ordinary virtues loudly and the brave act once, sideways. A shape:

"We are not going to make a speech about the commendation, because Craig has threatened to leave, and he's faster than all of us and knows the exits professionally.

One sentence, then. A man is alive tonight, eating his own dinner with his own family, because when the moment came, my brother did the thing he has quietly trained to do for fourteen years. That's the sentence. It's in the record. We move on.

What the rest of us actually live with, day to day, is the other Craig: the one who fixes everyone's boiler emergencies by phone, who turns up with a ladder before you've finished explaining, who is the calmest voice in any room that contains a smoke alarm and a drama.

The commendation is for one night. The ladder-and-calm is for us, every week, and it's the same man. Craig: we're proud past the point of embarrassment — yours and ours. Dinner."

"We move on" — announced in advance — is the mercy that lets him stay seated through the one sentence; a reluctant hero can endure anything with a known end. The ladder material then relocates the family's pride to the weekly version of him, which is praise he can accept because it's praise of usefulness, and usefulness is the only currency men like Craig recognise.

Our neighbours of 20 years are emigrating to Canada. The street is doing a farewell in the community hall. I've been asked to speak for the street. I want to say goodbye to the Hendersons in a way that celebrates them and doesn't just make everyone cry in a hall.

A street farewell should sound like a street: practical, funny, and full of tiny services. A shape:

"Twenty years the Hendersons have been at number seven, and the street has run on them in ways we are about to discover, to our cost. They hold the spare keys for four houses. They know the bin schedule, the good plumber, and which fence panels are whose responsibility, a matter of international law on this street.

Canada is getting, and I have written to warn them: a man who has mended more bikes than he owns, and a woman whose Christmas lights have been the street's official start of the season for two decades. December is going to be darker and we are all going to have to step up.

Hendersons: you are not leaving this street, exactly. You're extending it. There's a branch office now, in Ontario, and it will be inspected.

Go well. The keys, the plumber, and December are in our hands. Mostly."

"Extending the street" reframes emigration as expansion rather than subtraction — the room leaves feeling enlarged instead of diminished. Listing their functions (keys, plumber, lights) is the truest possible tribute for neighbours, because neighbourliness is a job description before it's a feeling, and hearing theirs read aloud tells them exactly what they were to the street.

My niece just lost her first tooth and there's a family video call tonight. She wants me — the fun uncle — to make a little speech about it. Yes, really. Give me something suitably grand for a six-year-old's tooth.

Grand is exactly right — a six-year-old's first tooth deserves full state ceremony. Forty seconds, maximum pomp:

"Ladies and gentlemen of the family, joining us from three kitchens and one car: we are gathered to mark a historic event. Today, at approximately lunchtime, Miss Lily Chen, aged six, lost her first tooth. It came out during an apple. The apple has been retained for questioning.

This tooth served with distinction. It bit through approximately four thousand sandwiches and at least one of my fingers. It will now be collected by the Tooth Fairy, who pays, I am told, well above inflation.

Lily: the gap is distinguished. The lisp is temporary. The money is yours.

Three cheers for the tooth."

For a child, the joke is the formality itself — adult ceremony aimed at a tiny event tells her the family takes her milestones seriously at full scale. Keep it under a minute, let her show the gap on camera at "the gap is distinguished," and have the family actually do the three cheers; participation is what she'll remember, not the words.

My friend Marta is celebrating 30 years since she arrived in this country as a refugee with nothing. She's hosting a dinner and asked me — her oldest friend here — to say a few words. I want to honour what she's built without making her story sound like a hardship lecture. She has a wicked sense of humour and a restaurant of her own now.

Let her humour set the register — her story told her way is a triumph with jokes, not a lecture. A shape:

"Thirty years ago Marta arrived in this country with one bag, no English, and — she would want this on the record — completely wrong shoes for the climate.

Within a year she had the language. Within five, the café job. Within ten, the café. I watched her negotiate her first lease in her second language with a landlord who described the experience afterwards as 'educational.' The restaurant some of you ate in tonight is the third thing she has built here, after the language and the life.

People like to call stories like Marta's inspiring, and she tolerates this, but I have her permission to correct it: she was not inspired. She was busy. There is a difference, and the difference is why it worked.

Marta: thirty years. Wrong shoes, right country. We're all so glad the buses brought you here."

"She was not inspired; she was busy" honours her agency instead of her suffering — the distinction refugees most often ask for and least often get at microphones. The shoes callback closes the arc from arrival to ownership in one image, and it is her joke, told with permission, which is the only way someone else's hardship humour is ever legitimate.

My work team has just won our industry's team of the year award — there were only nine of us up against big departments. There's a celebration lunch and as team lead I want to say a few words that share the credit properly and don't sound like an acceptance speech at the Oscars.

Nine people means you can name everyone — and naming everyone is the whole art of sharing credit. A shape:

"The award says 'team of the year,' and for once the paperwork is accurate, so let me do the roll call properly, because nine is a number you can honour in full.

This belongs to Amara, who rebuilt the rota nobody else would touch; to Ben, who answers the phone like every caller is the only caller; to Chris, Priya, Tom, and Zoe, who carried the winter peak without a single drama reaching the clients; to Sam, who trains every new starter into someone the rest of us rely on by month two; and to Jo, who has kept this team's humour and its spreadsheet alive with equal ferocity.

The big departments we beat have more people. They do not have these nine.

Team: it's ours, it says so on the trophy, and the trophy is going in the kitchen where it can supervise the biscuit tin. To us."

A roll call with one specific contribution per person takes ninety seconds and is worth more than any rhetoric about teamwork — each member hears their actual work named in public, once, on the record. Keep your own name out of the list entirely; the lead's credit is the arranging, and the room will notice the omission and credit you for it.

I'm giving the closing words at our town's remembrance concert — not a religious service, a community concert with the choir and school band. I need about two minutes that close the evening with dignity: gratitude to performers, a word about why we gather, nothing political.

Closing words at remembrance events should lower the temperature gently and hand the audience back to their own thoughts. A shape:

"Before we go, thank you: to the choir, who have sung this programme every year and make it new each time; to the school band, some of whom are playing tonight for relatives whose names are on the memorial — we see you, and we're proud of you; and to everyone who organised, ushered, baked, and stood in the cold with collection tins.

We gather like this because remembering is not something a town can leave to chance. It has to be practised, together, out loud, in rooms like this one, with music doing the parts that words do badly. The names on the memorial were people who expected to come home to ordinary life. The most faithful way to honour them is to keep that ordinary life worth coming home to — and to keep gathering, like this, to say so.

Thank you for coming. Travel home safely. We will do this again next year, because they are worth it, and because so is this town."

"Remembering has to be practised" gives the audience a reason the concert recurs that isn't habit — it makes attendance itself the tribute. Keep the close completely free of contemporary references; remembrance language ages badly when it borrows the week's news, and the school band sentence — one specific, human recognition — will do more for the room than any general gratitude.

My parents never had a wedding — they married at a register office in 1979 with two witnesses and went back to work. For their 45th anniversary we're throwing them the wedding party they never had, and I'm speaking. I want to honour the choice they made then and the party now, without implying their marriage was incomplete without a fuss.

The frame is: the party is our gift, not their lack. A shape:

"In 1979, my parents got married at the register office at half past nine in the morning, with two witnesses borrowed from the queue, and then they went back to work. Dad wore his good suit. Mum wore a dress she later used for christenings, ours included. There were no photographs, which is why tonight's photographer has been instructed to take approximately four hundred.

People sometimes hear that story and say 'what a shame.' I want to correct the record on their behalf. Nothing was missing in 1979. They had the only essential component, in full, and they have renewed it daily for forty-five years without an audience.

Tonight is not the wedding they missed. It's the party we owed them — the interest on forty-five years of watching them be quietly, completely right about what matters.

Mum, Dad: you did the marriage first and the wedding second, which we now agree is the correct order. Dance. You've had forty-five years to practise."

"The interest on forty-five years" reframes the party as the children's debt being paid, which protects the parents from any hint that their register office was a deficit. The borrowed-witnesses detail is worth keeping if true in spirit — it makes 1979 vivid and funny rather than austere, and the room laughs with admiration, which is the exact temperature this speech needs.

My best friend is having a baby shower this weekend and I've been asked to give a little toast. She's nervous about the birth and I want words that are joyful and calming, looking forward, not full of advice. Everyone gives her advice. I want to be the one who doesn't.

A no-advice toast is a gift in itself — say so in the toast, and it becomes the theme. A shape:

"I have a prepared statement: I am the only person at this shower who will offer Hannah no advice whatsoever. She has books, apps, a midwife, and a mother. What she doesn't have too much of is people simply saying: this is going to be wonderful and so are you.

So, my entire contribution: Hannah, you are the person our whole group rings when things fall apart. You are calm, you are funny at 3 a.m., and you have kept every one of us fed and sane through our own worst years. The baby is getting that person as a mother. I have thought about the odds and they are excellent.

Whatever the next few months hold, you will not hold them alone. This room is the evidence — we're already here, we're already fed, we're already yours.

To Hannah, and to the small person who has no idea how lucky the draw was."

"The baby is getting that person as a mother" is reassurance built from evidence rather than platitude — it reminds a nervous first-time mother of her own track record at exactly the moment she's doubting it. Ending on the room as evidence gives her something to look at while she's toasted: a crowd of people who are, demonstrably, already showing up.

My grandfather's war medals are being presented to our local museum — he's 99 and will be there in his wheelchair. The museum asked the family for a few words at the handover. I want something dignified and short that honours him without turning him into a monument while he's sitting right there.

Short, and spoken to him as much as about him — a living man at his own tribute needs address, not just description. A shape:

"These medals are going to the museum today, and Grandad has views about this, which he has expressed: he says they're heavy, the museum has a better shelf, and it's time other people carried them. Characteristically, he is right on all three counts.

He earned them between 1943 and 1945, in places he has described to this family in exactly eleven stories, all of which end with someone else being brave. What the medals don't record is the seventy-nine years since: the work, the family, the garden, the generations who grew up safe in a world he helped hand back.

The museum is getting the medals. The family keeps the man, a while longer, which has always been the better arrangement.

Grandad: the shelf is theirs. The stories stay ours. Thank you."

"The family keeps the man" is the line that stops him becoming a monument in his own presence — it tells the room, and him, where the real treasure sits. Keep the whole thing under two minutes and position yourself where he can see your face; at ninety-nine, speeches are partly lip-read, and a grandson facing him is worth more than any phrase.

I'm welcoming a new vicar to our parish at a welcome service — I'm the churchwarden. The congregation is elderly, loyal, and was sad to lose our last vicar of 20 years. I want words that welcome the newcomer warmly without pretending the grief for the old one isn't in the room.

Name the grief in one sentence and it stops competing with the welcome. A shape:

"Welcome services are a peculiar mixture, so let me be honest about the mixture. This congregation loved its last vicar for twenty years, and some of that love is in this room tonight wearing the face of sadness. That is not a problem to be managed. It's the sign of a healthy church — we attach, and attaching is the job.

Reverend Osei, you are not a replacement part. You're the next chapter, and a chapter is allowed to be different in tone. What we can promise you is this: a congregation that shows up — to services, to rotas, to each other. The kettle in the hall is older than most of the choir and it has never once failed. Neither, in our better moments, have we.

We will learn how you take your tea. You will learn our names, our hymns, and which pew creaks. Give us a year and this will be home.

Welcome. The kettle's on."

"A chapter is allowed to be different in tone" gives the newcomer permission to be herself, which is the thing a successor most needs to hear publicly in week one. The kettle, twice, does the parish's real theology: continuity in this congregation lives in its habits of care, and a warden naming the kettle tells the new vicar exactly where to find the heart of the place.

My daughter just won a scholarship to a music school — she's 14, a cellist. Family dinner to celebrate and I want a toast that celebrates her without putting pressure on her about the future. She's sensitive and I don't want 'this is just the beginning' hanging over her.

A pressure-free toast celebrates the present tense only — no futures, no expectations. A shape:

"To Rosa, who has won a scholarship to study the cello, which means a panel of experts listened to her play and wrote down, officially, what this family has known since she was nine: she is very good at this.

I am not going to say anything about the future, because tonight is not about the future. Tonight is about a girl who practised when it was boring, who played through the squeaky years without quitting, whose left hand has done more scales than the rest of us have done anything.

Rosa: the scholarship is theirs. The music was always yours. Tonight there's cake, and the cake has no expectations whatsoever.

To Rosa — play us something after dinner only if you want to. Not wanting to is also completely fine."

"The cake has no expectations whatsoever" is the joke that carries the whole parental message: this house celebrates without invoicing her for it. And the closing permission — not playing is fine — proves the toast's thesis in action; a sensitive fourteen-year-old hears the difference between being celebrated and being exhibited, and she will relax for the whole evening because of that last sentence.

I'm the outgoing president of our allotment association, handing over after 15 years. The AGM wants a farewell from me. The members are gardeners — practical people. I want to say goodbye properly, celebrate the plots, and hand over to the new president, Sheila, with grace.

Gardeners respect seasons and handovers — use the calendar of the place itself. A shape:

"Fifteen years I've held this role, which in allotment time is fifteen springs of optimism, fifteen summers of glut, and fifteen autumn arguments about the bonfire, all of which I have enjoyed and some of which I won.

When I started, we had a waiting list of three and a shed with a roof problem. We now have a waiting list of forty, a shed with a kettle, and a community plot that supplies the food bank every week from June to October. That was not me. That was forty-odd households treating a patch of rented earth like it mattered, because it does.

Sheila takes over from tonight. She has better tomatoes than me, better minutes than me, and the same intolerance for plot-holders who let the weeds seed onto their neighbours, which is the only qualification that truly counts.

I'll still be on plot nine, available for advice, manure, and being wrong about frost dates. The association is in good hands. They're hers. Mind the paths, everyone."

"Available for advice, manure, and being wrong about frost dates" gives the room a laughing image of your retirement that keeps you inside the community while out of the chair — the graceful exit every long-serving volunteer hopes for. Handing over with one specific compliment and one shared value (the weed rule) tells members the continuity is real, which is all an AGM actually needs to hear.

I'm running my mum's 70th birthday and I want to give the evening a proper shape. Can you lay out a short programme for the celebration — order of events with my MC words at each point? About 60 guests, dinner, two speeches besides mine, and a surprise slideshow.

Here is a programme with a spine, and your exact words at each joint:

| Time | Event | Your words |
|---|---|---|
| 19:00 | Guests seated, Mum enters | "She has arrived, seventy years young and pretending she doesn't love this. Please stand for the guest of honour, Margaret." |
| 19:10 | Your welcome | "Seventy years, sixty guests, one woman who has fed most of this room at some point. Tonight the room feeds her. Welcome." |
| 20:00 | First speech, her brother | "Our first speaker knew her before any of us, and has the photographs to prove it. Her brother, Uncle Ray." |
| 20:45 | The surprise slideshow | "What follows was assembled in secret, from attics. Mum: denials will be entered into the record and ignored, as usual." |
| 21:15 | Second speech, her best friend | "Fifty years of friendship earns the floor. Her oldest friend, Dorothy." |
| 21:45 | Mum replies, cake, music | "The last word belongs, as it has since roughly 1956, to Mum. Then cake, then dancing, in that order, by law." |

Three choices give the evening its shape. Mum enters to a standing room — it costs nothing and it frames the night as hers. The slideshow sits between the speeches, not after them, because images reset a room's attention and the second speaker deserves a fresh audience. And Mum closes: at seventy, the guest of honour taking the last word is not a courtesy, it's the point of the gathering. Keep your own links under twenty seconds each; the MC's discipline is what lets everyone else's warmth expand.
